Configure S3 Block Public Access settings for the S3 bucket to allow only encrypted connections over HTTPS.
questions.explanation: Encrypting personal-data objects on the client side with a customer managed KMS key before they leave the application meets the on-demand key rotation requirement, since the company fully controls that key's rotation, and a bucket policy denying requests when aws:SecureTransport is false enforces HTTPS-only access, covering encryption in transit. A bucket policy cannot 'enable client-side encryption' since that happens in application code before upload (A, B), and Block Public Access settings (E) control public accessibility rather than the transport protocol used.

questions.question: A company has a monolithic desktop-based application that processes images. A developer is converting the application into an AWS Lambda function by using Python. Currently, the desktop application runs every 5 minutes to process the latest image from an Amazon S3 bucket. The desktop application completes the image processing task within 1 minute. During testing on AWS, the developer notices that the Lambda function runs at the specified 5-minute interval. However, the Lambda function takes more than 2 minutes to complete the image processing task. The developer needs a solution that will improve the Lambda function's performance. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Update the instance type of the Lambda function to a compute optimized instance with at least eight virtual CPU (vCPU).
Update the configuration of the Lambda function to use the latest Python runtime.
Increase the memory that is allocated to the Lambda function.
Configure a reserved concurrency on the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Increasing the memory allocated to the Lambda function proportionally increases the CPU power available to it (Lambda scales vCPU allocation with configured memory), which directly speeds up a CPU-bound image processing workload that is currently taking longer than expected. There is no 'instance type' or vCPU quota setting to configure directly on a Lambda function (A), updating to the latest Python runtime (B) is unlikely to meaningfully change a compute-bound task's duration on its own, and reserved concurrency (D) controls how many concurrent invocations are allowed, it does not make any single invocation run faster.

questions.question: A company uses AWS CloudFormation templates to manage infrastructure for a public-facing application in its development, pre-production, and production environments. The company needs to scale for increasing customer demand. A developer must upgrade the Amazon RDS DB instance type to a larger instance. The developer deploys an update to the CloudFormation stack with the instance size change in the pre-production environment. The developer notices that the stack is in an UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED slate in CloudFormation. Which option is the cause of this issue?
options: The new instance type specified in the CloudFormation template is invalid
The database was deleted or modified manually outside of the CloudFormation stack
There is a syntax error in the CloudFormation template
The developer has insufficient IAM permissions to provision an instance of the specified type
questions.explanation: An UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state commonly occurs when CloudFormation's automatic rollback tries to restore a resource to its previous state but finds that resource (here, the RDS database) was changed manually outside of CloudFormation, so CloudFormation's expected prior configuration no longer matches reality and the rollback cannot complete cleanly. An invalid instance type (A) or a template syntax error (C) would typically cause the initial update itself to fail outright rather than specifically produce a rollback-failed state after rollback has already been attempted, and insufficient IAM permissions (D) would generally surface as an access-denied error during the update attempt rather than this specific rollback failure state.

questions.question: A developer needs to store files in an Amazon S3 bucket for a company's application. Each S3 object can have multiple versions. The objects must be permanently removed 1 year after object creation. The developer creates an S3 bucket that has versioning enabled. What should the developer do next to meet the data retention requirements?
options: Create an S3 Lifecycle rule on the S3 bucket. Configure the rule to expire current versions of objects and permanently delete noncurrent versions 1 year after object creation.

Create an event notification for all object creation events in the S3 bucket. Configure the event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function. Program the Lambda function to check the object creation date and to delete the object if the object is older than 1 year.

Create an event notification for all object removal events in the S3 bucket. Configure the event notification to invoke an AWS Lambda function. Program the Lambda function to check the object creation date and to delete the object if the object is older than 1 year.
Create an S3 Lifecycle rule on the S3 bucket. Configure the rule to delete expired object delete markers and permanently delete noncurrent versions 1 year after object creation.
questions.explanation: An S3 Lifecycle rule configured to expire current versions and to permanently delete noncurrent versions after 1 year is the native, built-in mechanism to enforce this exact retention policy across all versions automatically, with no custom code. Building event-driven Lambda functions to check object age and delete objects on creation or removal events (B, C) reimplements what a Lifecycle rule already provides, and deleting expired delete markers and noncurrent versions (D) is a valid Lifecycle configuration concept but does not directly express expiring the current version itself after 1 year the way option A's rule does.

questions.question: A company uses AWS X-Ray to monitor a serverless application. The components of the application have different request rates. The user interactions and transactions are important to trace, but they are low in volume. The background processes such as application health checks, polling, and connection maintenance generate high volumes of read-only requests. Currently, the default X-Ray sampling rules are universal for all requests. Only the first request per second and some additional requests are recorded. This setup is not helping the company review the requests based on service or request type. A developer must configure rules to trace requests based on service or request properties. The developer must trace the user interactions and transactions without wasting effort recording minor background tasks. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Disable sampling for high-volume read-only requests. Sample at a lower rate for all requests that handle user interactions or transactions.
Disable sampling and trace all requests for requests that handle user interactions or transactions. Sample high-volume read-only requests at a higher rate.
Disable sampling and trace all requests for requests that handle user interactions or transactions. Sample high-volume read-only requests at a lower rate.
Disable sampling for high-volume read-only requests. Sample at a higher rate for all requests that handle user interactions or transactions.
questions.explanation: Custom sampling rules let the team trace every user interaction and transaction while keeping only a small fraction of high-volume health-check and polling traffic, matching cost to value. The inverse assignments in the other options either discard important transactions or retain excessive background noise.

questions.question: A developer uses an AWS Lambda function in an application to edit users' uploaded photos. The developer needs to update the Lambda function code and needs to test the updates. For testing, the developer must divide the user traffic between the original version of the Lambda function and the new version of the Lambda function. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Publish a version of the original Lambda function. Make the necessary changes to the Lambda code. Publish a new version of the Lambda function.

Use AWS CodeBuild to detect updates to the Lambda function. Configure CodeBuild to incrementally shift traffic from the original version of the Lambda function to the new version of the Lambda function.
Update the original version of the Lambda function to add a function URL. Make the necessary changes to the Lambda code. Publish another function URL for the updated Lambda code.

Create an alias that points to the original version of the Lambda function. Configure the alias to be a weighted alias that also includes the new version of the Lambda function. Divide traffic between the two versions.
Create an alias that points to the original function URL. Configure the alias to be a weighted alias that also includes the additional function URL. Divide traffic between the two function URLs.
questions.explanation: Publishing a version of the original Lambda function and then a new version with the necessary code changes gives two distinct, stable versions to route between, and creating an alias that points to the original version while also being configured as a weighted alias including the new version lets traffic be split between them using Lambda's native, purpose-built weighted-alias mechanism. Using CodeBuild to detect Lambda updates and shift traffic (B) is not a real CodeBuild capability, since CodeBuild builds and tests code rather than managing Lambda invocation routing, and creating and weighting two separate Lambda function URLs (C, E) is not how Lambda function URLs work, they don't support built-in weighted traffic splitting the way aliases do.

questions.question: A company had an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance that was named mysql-db. The DB instance was deleted within the past 90 days. A developer needs to find which IAM user or role deleted the DB instance in the AWS environment. Which solution will provide this information?
options: Retrieve the AWS CloudTrail events for the resource mysql-db where the event name is DeleteDBInstance. Inspect each event.
Retrieve the Amazon CloudWatch log events from the most recent log stream within the rds/mysql-db log group. Inspect the log events.
Retrieve the AWS X-Ray trace summaries. Filter by services with the name mysql-db. Inspect the ErrorRootCauses values within each summary.
Retrieve the AWS Systems Manager deletions inventory. Filter the inventory by deletions that have a TypeName value of RDS. Inspect the deletion details.
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records management events including DeleteDBInstance with the identity that made the call, and events are retained and searchable for the past 90 days. RDS database logs capture engine activity rather than who deleted the instance; X-Ray traces application requests rather than control-plane deletions; Systems Manager inventory tracks managed-instance software, not RDS deletions.

questions.question: A company has an ecommerce web application that uses an on-premises MySQL database as a data store. The company migrates the on-premises MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. A developer needs to configure the application's access to the RDS for MySQL database. The developer's solution must not use long term credentials. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Enable IAM database authentication on the RDS for MySQL DB instance. Create an IAM role that has the minimum required permissions. Assign the role to the application.
Store the MySQL credentials as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager. Create an IAM role that has the minimum required permissions to retrieve the secrets. Assign the role to the application.
Configure the MySQL credentials as environment variables that are available at runtime for the application.

Store the MySQL credentials as SecureString parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Create an IAM role that has the minimum required permissions to retrieve the parameters. Assign the role to the application.
questions.explanation: IAM database authentication lets applications authenticate to RDS using short-lived, auto-generated tokens tied to an IAM role rather than a static database password, directly meeting the 'no long term credentials' requirement. Storing MySQL credentials, even securely, in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store (B, D) still uses a long-term database password under the hood, and plain environment variables (C) store the password in plaintext with no rotation.

questions.question: A developer is creating an application that must transfer expired items from Amazon DynamoDB to Amazon S3. The developer sets up the DynamoDB table to automatically delete items after a specific TTL. The application must process the items in DynamoDB and then must store the expired items in Amazon S3. The entire process, including item processing and storage in Amazon S3, will take 5 minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to query for expired items based on the TTL. Save the results to Amazon S3.
Configure DynamoDB Streams to invoke an AWS Lambda function. Program the Lambda function to process the items and to store the expired items in Amazon S3.

Deploy a custom application on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster on Amazon EC2 instances. Program the custom application to process the items and to store the expired items in Amazon S3.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function. Program the Lambda function to process the items and to store the expired items in Amazon S3.
questions.explanation: Configuring DynamoDB Streams on the table to invoke a Lambda function when TTL expires items lets the Lambda function process each expiring item and write it to S3 as it is removed, entirely event-driven with no infrastructure to manage beyond the function itself, the least operational overhead. DynamoDB Accelerator (A) is a read-caching layer, not a mechanism for querying or reacting to expired items, running a custom application on an ECS/EC2 cluster (C) requires standing up and managing compute infrastructure that a Lambda trigger avoids, and a separately scheduled EventBridge rule invoking a Lambda function to scan for expired items (D) duplicates work that DynamoDB Streams already delivers automatically when TTL deletes occur.

questions.question: A developer has an application that uses WebSocket APIs in Amazon API Gateway. The developer wants to use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer to control access to the application. The developer needs to add credential caching and reduce repeated usage of secret keys and authorization tokens on every request. Which combination of steps should the developer take to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Use a token-based Lambda authorizer.
Use a request parameter-based Lambda authorizer.
Configure an integration request mapping template to reference the context map from the APIGateway Lambda authorizer.
Configure an integration request mapping template to reference the identity API key value from the API Gateway Lambda authorizer.
Use VPC endpoint policies for the WebSocket APIs.
questions.explanation: A REQUEST-type Lambda authorizer can cache its authorization result based on the specified request parameters rather than a single bearer token, reducing repeated invocation, and referencing the authorizer's returned context map in the integration request mapping template lets the backend reuse the already-validated authorization data instead of resending credentials on every call. A token-based authorizer (A) caches only by a single incoming token, referencing just an identity API key value (D) is narrower than the full context map, and VPC endpoint policies (E) control network-level access rather than authorizer credential caching.

questions.question: A developer builds a serverless application on AWS by using Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda functions, and Amazon Route 53. During testing, the developer notices errors but cannot immediately locate the root cause. To identify the errors, the developer needs to search all the application's logs. What should the developer do to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Set up API Gateway health checks to monitor the application's availability. Use the Amazon CloudWatch PutMetricData API operation to publish the logs to CloudWatch. Search and query the logs by using Amazon Athena.

Set up Route 53 health checks to monitor the application's availability. Turn on AWS CloudTrail logs for all the AWS services that the application uses. Send the logs to a specified Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the log files directly from Amazon S3.

Configure all the application's AWS services to publish a real-time feed of log events to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the delivery stream to publish all the logs to an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service to search and analyze the logs.

Set up Route 53 health checks to monitor the application's availability. Turn on Amazon CloudWatch Logs for the API Gateway stages to log API requests with a JSON log format. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to search and analyze the logs from the AWS services that the application uses.
questions.explanation: API Gateway stages can emit execution and access logs to CloudWatch Logs in JSON, and Logs Insights then searches across the application log groups with the least infrastructure to run. Health checks only report availability; CloudTrail plus Athena over S3 is heavier and targets API audit history; Kinesis Firehose plus OpenSearch adds streaming and search-cluster overhead.

questions.question: A developer needs to freeze changes to an AWS CodeCommit repository before a production release. The developer will work on new features while a quality assurance (QA) team tests the release. The QA testing and all bug fixes must take place in isolation from the main branch. After the release, the developer must integrate all bug fixes into the main branch. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a release branch from the latest Git commit that will be in the release. Apply fixes to the release branch. Continue developing new features, and merge the features into the main branch. Merge the release branch into the main branch after the release.

Create a Git tag on the latest Git commit that will be in the release. Continue developing new features, and merge the features into the main branch. Apply fixes to the main branch. Update the Git tag for the release to be on the latest commit on the main branch.

Create a release branch from the latest Git commit that will be in the release. Apply fixes to the release branch. Continue developing new features, and merge the features into the main branch. Rebase the main branch onto the release branch after the release.

Create a Git tag on the latest Git commit that will be in the release. Continue developing new features, and merge the features into the main branch. Apply the Git commits for fixes to the Git tag for the release.
questions.explanation: Creating a release branch from the exact commit that will ship, applying bug fixes directly to that isolated release branch while new feature development continues independently on the main branch, and merging the release branch's fixes back into main after the release, cleanly isolates QA testing and bug fixing from ongoing feature work while ensuring fixes eventually make it into the main line of development. Using a Git tag instead of a branch (B, D) only marks a single commit and provides no separate, independently committable line of work for applying and isolating bug fixes, and rebasing main onto the release branch after release (C) would effectively discard or reorder the new feature commits made on main, which is not the intended outcome.

questions.question: A developer is setting up AWS CodePipeline for a new application. During each build, the developer must generate a test report. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Create an AWS CodeBuild build project that runs tests. Configure the buildspec file with the test report information.
Create an AWS CodeDeploy deployment that runs tests. Configure the AppSpec file with the test report information.
Run the builds on an Amazon EC2 instance that has AWS Systems Manager Agent (SSM Agent) installed and activated.
Create a repository in AWS CodeArtifact. Select the test report template.
questions.explanation: Creating a CodeBuild project that runs the tests, with the buildspec file configured to include the test report information (using CodeBuild's built-in reports section), natively generates a test report as part of each CodePipeline build with no separate reporting tool required. CodeDeploy (B) is a deployment service rather than a test-execution and reporting tool, running builds on a self-managed EC2 instance with SSM Agent (C) reimplements a managed build service that CodeBuild already provides natively including report generation, and CodeArtifact (D) is a package repository, it has no built-in test report template capability.

questions.question: A developer built an application by using multiple AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda functions must access dynamic configuration data at runtime. The data is maintained as a 6 KB JSON document in AWS AppConfig. The configuration data needs to be updated without requiring the redeployment of the application. The developer needs a solution that will give the Lambda functions access to the dynamic configuration data. What should the developer do to meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
options: Migrate the document from AWS AppConfig to a Lambda environment variable. Read the document at the runtime.
Configure the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension. Access the dynamic configuration data by calling the extension on a local host.
Use the AWS X-Ray SDK to call the AWS AppConfig APIs. Retrieve the configuration file at runtime.
Migrate the configuration file to a Lambda deployment package. Read the file from the file system at runtime.
questions.explanation: The AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension runs alongside the function, caching and serving the configuration data over a local HTTP endpoint (localhost), so Lambda functions can retrieve the latest AppConfig data with a simple local call and no custom polling logic, and configuration updates in AppConfig are picked up without any code redeployment. Migrating the document into a Lambda environment variable (A) would require redeploying the function every time the configuration changes, which contradicts the requirement, using the X-Ray SDK to call AppConfig APIs (C) misapplies X-Ray, which is a tracing service, not a configuration retrieval mechanism, and bundling the configuration file into the deployment package (D) again requires a redeployment for every configuration change.

questions.question: A developer has AWS Lambda functions that need to access a company's internal data science libraries and reference data. Separate teams manage the libraries and the data. The teams must be able to update and upload new data independently. The Lambda functions are connected to the company's central VPC. Which solution will provide the Lambda functions with access to the libraries and data?
options: Attach an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume to the Lambda functions by using EBS Multi-Attach in the central VPC. Update the Lambda function execution roles to give the functions to access the EBS volume. Update the Lambda function code to reference the files in the EBS volume.
Compress the libraries and reference data in a Lambda /tmp folder. Update the Lambda function code to reference the files in the /tmp folder.

Set up an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system with mount targets in the central VPConfigure the Lambda functions to mount the EFS file system. Update the Lambda function execution roles to give the functions to access the EFS file system.

Set up an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system with mount targets in the central VPC. Configure the Lambda functions to mount the Amazon FSx file system. Update the Lambda function execution roles to give the functions to access the Amazon FSx file system.
questions.explanation: An Amazon EFS file system with mount targets in the central VPC, mounted by the Lambda functions (with the execution role granted the needed EFS access permissions), gives every function shared, low-latency, POSIX file access to the libraries and reference data, and separate teams can update files on the shared file system independently without redeploying any Lambda function. EBS Multi-Attach (A) is limited to specific Nitro-based EC2 instance types and is not usable by Lambda, compressing everything into the ephemeral /tmp folder (B) does not provide a shared location that other teams can update independently, and Amazon FSx for Windows File Server (D) uses the SMB protocol, which is not natively supported by the Lambda service the way EFS's NFS-based mounting is.

questions.question: A company has an application that uses an AWS Lambda function to consume messages from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The SQS queue is configured with a dead-letter queue. Due to a defect in the application, AWS Lambda failed to process some messages. A developer fixed the bug and wants to process the failed messages again. How should the developer resolve this issue?
options: Use the SendMessageBatch API to send messages from the dead-letter queue to the original SQS queue.
Use the ChangeMessageVisibility API to configure messages in the dead-letter queue to be visible in the original SQS queue.
Use the StartMessageMoveTask API to move messages from the dead-letter queue to the original SQS queue.
Use the PurgeQueue API to remove messages from the dead-letter queue and return the messages to the original SQS queue.
questions.explanation: The SQS StartMessageMoveTask API is purpose-built to move messages from a dead-letter queue back to its original source queue (or another destination) asynchronously and at a configurable rate, which is exactly the documented mechanism for reprocessing failed messages after fixing the underlying bug. SendMessageBatch (A) would require manually reading each DLQ message and re-sending it, which StartMessageMoveTask automates, ChangeMessageVisibility (B) only affects visibility timing within a single queue, it does not move messages between queues, and PurgeQueue (D) permanently deletes all messages in a queue, which would destroy the failed messages rather than reprocess them.

questions.question: A developer is working on an application that will be deployed on AWS. The developer needs to test and debug the code locally. The code is packaged and stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. How can the developer test and debug the code locally with the LEAST amount of configuration?
options: Create an application and a deployment group in AWS CodeDeploy. For the compute platform, specify the local machine as the individual instance for the deployment. For the repository type, specify that the application is stored in Amazon S3. Start the deployment to test on the local machine.
Create a repository in AWS CodeArtifact. Publish the application code package to the repository. Before deployment, create an upstream repository to test and validate the code.

Create a build project in AWS CodeBuild. In AWS CodePipeline, add a CodeBuild test action by adding a stage and an action. For the action provider, specify a CodeBuild test and the build project. View the build log to see the test results.

Install the AWS CodeDeploy agent locally to validate the deployment package. Run the codedeploy-local command. Specify the S3 bucket where the code package is located by using the --bundle-location option.
questions.explanation: Installing the CodeDeploy agent locally and running the codedeploy-local command with the --bundle-location option pointing at the S3-hosted deployment package lets the developer simulate and run an actual CodeDeploy deployment directly on their own machine, with the least configuration since it reuses the exact same deployment package and agent used in real deployments. Setting up a full CodeDeploy application and deployment group targeting the 'local machine as an individual instance' (A) is more configuration than simply invoking the agent's local testing command directly, and standing up a CodeBuild project and CodePipeline stage (C) or publishing through CodeArtifact (B) both introduce pipeline infrastructure unnecessary for a quick local debug test.

questions.question: A developer is creating an application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). The developer needs to configure the application parameters. The developer must configure limits for the application's maximum number of simultaneous connections and maximum number of transactions per second. The maximum number of connections and transactions can change in the future. The developer needs a solution that can automatically deploy these changes to the application, as needed, without causing downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Make the configuration changes for the application. Use AWS CodeDeploy to create a deployment configuration. Specify an in-place deployment to deploy the changes.

Bootstrap the application to use the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) and make the configuration changes. Specify the ECSCanary10Percent15Minutes launch type in the properties section of the ECS resource. Deploy the application by using the AWS CDK to implement the changes.

Install the AWS AppConfig agent on Amazon ECS. Configure an IAM role with access to AWS AppConfig. Make the deployment changes by using AWS AppConfig. Specify Canary10Percent20Minutes as the deployment strategy.

Create an AWS Lambda function to make the configuration changes. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that monitors the Lambda function every 5 minutes to check if the Lambda function has been updated. When the Lambda function is updated, deploy the changes by using AWS CodeDeploy.
questions.explanation: Installing the AWS AppConfig agent on the ECS tasks, granting an IAM role with AppConfig access, and using AppConfig with a predefined gradual deployment strategy like Canary10Percent20Minutes lets configuration limits (like connection and transaction thresholds) be updated and safely, automatically rolled out to the running application with no downtime and no application redeployment, exactly matching a value that may change again in the future. Using CodeDeploy's in-place deployment (A) or the AWS CDK with an ECS-specific 'canary launch type property' that does not actually exist (B) both describe redeploying the application itself rather than dynamically updating a runtime configuration value, and building a custom Lambda function polled by a CloudWatch alarm every 5 minutes (D) reimplements what AppConfig's managed deployment and validation mechanism already provides natively.

questions.question: A developer has built an application running on AWS Lambda using AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM). What is the correct sequence of steps to successfully deploy the application?
options: 1. Build the SAM template in Amazon EC2. 2. Package the SAM template to Amazon EBS storage. 3. Deploy the SAM template from Amazon EBS.
1. Build the SAM template locally. 2. Package the SAM template onto Amazon S3. 3. Deploy the SAM template from Amazon S3.
1. Build the SAM template locally. 2. Deploy the SAM template from Amazon S3. 3. Package the SAM template for use.
1. Build the SAM template locally. 2. Package the SAM template from AWS CodeCommit. 3. Deploy the SAM template to CodeCommit.
questions.explanation: The correct AWS SAM workflow is to first build the application locally (sam build), then package it by uploading the built artifacts to an Amazon S3 bucket (sam package), and finally deploy the packaged template from that S3 location (sam deploy), which transforms the SAM template into a CloudFormation stack. Building on EC2 and packaging to EBS storage (A) misrepresents SAM's actual workflow, which uses S3 for packaged artifacts rather than an attached EBS volume, deploying before packaging (C) is out of order since deployment needs the already-packaged S3 artifacts, and packaging from or deploying to CodeCommit (D) confuses a source-control repository with the S3-based artifact packaging step SAM actually uses.

questions.question: A developer needs to deploy the code for a new application on an AWS Lambda function. The application needs a dependency file that is 500 MB to run the business logic. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Compress the application code and dependencies into a .zip file. Directly upload the .zip file as a deployment package for the Lambda function instead of copying the code.
Compress the application code and dependencies into a .zip file. Upload the .zip file to an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the Lambda function to run the code from the .zip file in the S3 bucket.
Package the application code and dependencies into a container image. Upload the image to an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the Lambda function to run the code in the image.
Package the application code and dependencies into a container image. Push the image to an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Deploy the image to the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Compressing the code and the 500 MB dependency into a .zip file and uploading it to an S3 bucket, with the Lambda function configured to deploy from that S3 location, accommodates a package well beyond the 50 MB direct-console-upload limit (Lambda's .zip deployment package limit from S3 is up to 250 MB unzipped), matching the size described. Directly uploading a large .zip file to the Lambda console (A) is limited to a much smaller size than deploying from S3, and packaging the code as a container image and pointing at it via an S3 bucket (C) is not how Lambda container images work, since Lambda container images are deployed from Amazon ECR, not S3.

questions.question: A company is developing a publicly accessible single-page application. The application makes calls from a client web browser to backend services to provide a user interface to customers. The application depends on a third-party web service exposed as an HTTP API. The web client must provide an API key to the third-party web service by using the HTTP header as part of the HTTP request. The company's API key must not be exposed to the users of the web application. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Use Amazon API Gateway to create a private REST API. Create an HTTP integration to integrate with the third-party HTTP API. Add the company’s API key to the HTTP headers list of the integration request configuration.

Use Amazon API Gateway to create a private REST API. Create an AWS Lambda proxy integration. Make calls to the third-party HTTP API from the Lambda function. Pass the company's API key as an HTTP request header.

Use Amazon API Gateway to create a REST API. Create an HTTP integration to integrate with the third-party HTTP API. Add the company's API key to the HTTP headers list of the integration request configuration.

Use Amazon API Gateway to create a REST API. Create an AWS Lambda proxy integration. Make calls to the third-party HTTP API from the Lambda function. Pass the company's API key as an HTTP request header.
questions.explanation: Using Amazon API Gateway to create a (regular, non-private) REST API with an AWS Lambda proxy integration lets the Lambda function's backend code hold and use the company's API key when calling the third-party service, so the key never reaches the client browser, and a REST API with Lambda proxy integration is a straightforward, cost-effective way to build this backend layer. A private REST API (A, B) restricts access to within a VPC, which does not fit a publicly accessible single-page application's client calls, and adding the API key directly into an HTTP integration's request headers (A, C) exposes the key's presence and value in the API's own configuration in a way that is less clearly isolated from the client-facing request path than routing the call through Lambda's own backend code.

questions.question: A developer is setting up the deployment of application stacks to new test environments by using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK). The application contains the code for several AWS Lambda functions that will be deployed as assets. Each Lambda function is defined by using the AWS CDK Lambda construct library. The developer has already successfully deployed the application stacks to the alpha environment in the first account by using the AWS CDK CLI's cdk deploy command. The developer is preparing to deploy to the beta environment in a second account for the first time. The developer makes no significant changes to the CDK code between deployments, but the initial deployment in the second account is unsuccessful and returns a NoSuchBucket error. Which command should the developer run before redeployment to resolve this error?
options: cdk synth
cdk bootstrap
cdk init
cdk destroy
questions.explanation: Running cdk bootstrap in the new (second) AWS account provisions the foundational resources the CDK CLI needs, most notably an S3 bucket for storing deployment assets like Lambda function code, so a NoSuchBucket error on a first-ever deployment to a new account specifically indicates that account has not yet been bootstrapped. cdk synth (A) only generates the CloudFormation template locally, it doesn't provision any account resources, cdk init (C) scaffolds a brand-new CDK project rather than preparing an account for deployment, and cdk destroy (D) tears down an already-deployed stack, which is the opposite of what's needed here.

questions.question: A developer is automating a new application deployment with AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM). The new application has one AWS Lambda function and one Amazon S3 bucket. The Lambda function must access the S3 bucket to only read objects. How should the developer configure AWS SAM to grant the necessary read privilege to the S3 bucket?
options: Reference a second Lambda authorizer function.
Add a custom S3 bucket policy to the Lambda function.
Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) topic for only S3 object reads. Reference the topic in the template.
Add the S3ReadPolicy template to the Lambda function's execution role.
questions.explanation: Adding the S3ReadPolicy SAM policy template to the Lambda function's execution role is AWS SAM's built-in, purpose-built shorthand for granting exactly read-only access to a specified S3 bucket, requiring no custom IAM policy JSON to write. Referencing a second Lambda authorizer function (A) is unrelated to granting S3 read access, adding a custom bucket policy is more manual configuration than using SAM's managed policy template (B), and creating an SQS topic for S3 reads (C) is not a real mechanism, since SQS is a queue service, not an access-control layer for S3.

questions.question: A development team wants to immediately build and deploy an application whenever there is a change to the source code. Which approaches could be used to trigger the deployment? (Choose two.)
options: Store the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure AWS CodePipeline to start whenever a file in the bucket changes.
Store the source code in an encrypted Amazon EBS volume. Configure AWS CodePipeline to start whenever a file in the volume changes.
Store the source code in an AWS CodeCommit repository. Configure AWS CodePipeline to start whenever a change is committed to the repository.
Store the source code in an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure AWS CodePipeline to start every 15 minutes.
Store the source code in an Amazon EC2 instance’s ephemeral storage. Configure the instance to start AWS CodePipeline whenever there are changes to the source code.
questions.explanation: Storing source code in a CodeCommit repository with CodePipeline configured to start on a commit to the repository, or storing it in an S3 bucket with CodePipeline configured to start when a file in the bucket changes, are both native, event-driven CodePipeline source configurations that trigger a pipeline run immediately upon a code change, requiring no polling or manual triggers. Storing source code on an EBS volume (B) or in EC2 instance ephemeral storage (E) are not supported CodePipeline source types at all, and a fixed 15-minute polling schedule (D) introduces unnecessary delay compared to immediate, event-driven triggering.

questions.question: A developer is building an application integrating an Amazon API Gateway with an AWS Lambda function. When calling the API, the developer receives the following error: Wed Nov 08 01:13:00 UTC 2017 : Method completed with status: 502 What should the developer do to resolve the error?
options: Change the HTTP endpoint of the API to an HTTPS endpoint.
Change the format of the payload sent to the API Gateway.
Change the format of the Lambda function response to the API call.
Change the authorization header in the API call to access the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: An HTTP 502 Bad Gateway from API Gateway when integrated with Lambda typically means the Lambda function's response was not in the format API Gateway expects (for example, a malformed proxy integration response), so fixing the Lambda function's response format resolves it. Changing the API's endpoint from HTTP to HTTPS (A) is unrelated to a 502 caused by integration response formatting, changing the format of the request payload sent to the API (B) addresses input rather than the output formatting issue causing the 502, and changing the authorization header (D) would more likely produce a 401/403 error rather than a 502.

questions.question: A developer is building various microservices for an application that will run on Amazon EC2 instances. The developer needs to monitor the end-to-end view of the requests between the microservices and debug any issues in the various microservices. What should the developer do to accomplish these tasks?
options: Use Amazon CloudWatch to aggregate the microservices' logs and metrics, and build the monitoring dashboard.
Use AWS CloudTrail to aggregate the microservices' logs and metrics, and build the monitoring dashboard.
Use the AWS X-Ray SDK to add instrumentation in all the microservices, and monitor using the X-Ray service map.
Use AWS Health to monitor the health of all the microservices.
questions.explanation: Adding the X-Ray SDK to each microservice emits segments that X-Ray assembles into a service map showing the end-to-end request path and per-hop faults. CloudWatch aggregates logs and metrics but not the linked request graph; CloudTrail audits AWS API usage rather than inter-service calls; Health reports AWS service events rather than application topology.

questions.question: A developer is building a microservice that uses AWS Lambda to process messages from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue. The Lambda function calls external APIs to enrich the SQS message data before loading the data into an Amazon Redshift data warehouse. The SQS queue must handle a maximum of 1,000 messages per second. During initial testing, the Lambda function repeatedly inserted duplicate data into the Amazon Redshift table. The duplicate data led to a problem with data analysis. All duplicate messages were submitted to the queue within 1 minute of each other. How should the developer resolve this issue?
options: Create an SQS FIFO queue. Enable message deduplication on the SQS FIFO queue.
Reduce the maximum Lambda concurrency that the SQS queue can invoke.
Use Lambda's temporary storage to keep track of processed message identifiers
Configure a message group ID for every sent message. Enable message deduplication on the SQS standard queue.
questions.explanation: Creating an SQS FIFO queue with message deduplication enabled ensures that messages submitted within the deduplication interval (a 5-minute window) that have identical content (or an explicit deduplication ID) are treated as duplicates and only delivered once, directly preventing the duplicate Redshift inserts described, while a FIFO queue's higher throughput limits can still comfortably handle 1,000 messages per second with high throughput mode. Reducing Lambda concurrency (B) does not address duplicate messages already in the queue, using Lambda's temporary storage to track processed IDs (C) requires building custom deduplication logic that FIFO's native deduplication already provides, and message group IDs (D) control ordering within a FIFO queue, they do not by themselves enable deduplication on a standard queue.

questions.question: A company has an application that uses an Amazon API Gateway API to invoke an AWS Lambda function. The application is latency sensitive. A developer needs to configure the Lambda function to reduce the cold start time that is associated with default scaling. What should the developer do to meet these requirements?
options: Publish a new version of the Lambda function. Configure provisioned concurrency. Set the provisioned concurrency limit to meet the company requirements.
Increase the Lambda function's memory to the maximum amount. Increase the Lambda function's reserved concurrency limit.
Increase the reserved concurrency of the Lambda function to a number that matches the current production load.
Use Service Quotas to request an increase in the Lambda function's concurrency limit for the AWS account where the function is deployed.
questions.explanation: Publishing a version of the Lambda function and configuring provisioned concurrency on it pre-initializes a specified number of execution environments ahead of invocations, eliminating the cold start latency associated with default on-demand scaling, directly addressing the requirement. Simply increasing memory and reserved concurrency (B) can improve a warm invocation's runtime but does not eliminate cold starts the way pre-warmed, provisioned environments do, increasing reserved concurrency alone to match production load (C) reserves capacity but still leaves new environments to cold-start when scaling beyond what's already warm, and raising the account's overall concurrency limit via Service Quotas (D) increases how much the function can scale, it does not reduce the latency of any individual cold start.

questions.question: A developer is deploying an application on Amazon EC2 instances that run in Account A. The application needs to read data from an existing Amazon Kinesis data stream in Account B. Which actions should the developer take to provide the application with access to the stream? (Choose two.)
options: Update the instance profile role in Account A with stream read permissions.
Create an IAM role with stream read permissions in Account B.
Add a trust policy to the instance profile role and IAM role in Account B to allow the instance profile role to assume the IAM role.
Add a trust policy to the instance profile role and IAM role in Account B to allow reads from the stream.
Add a resource-based policy in Account B to allow read access from the instance profile role.
questions.explanation: Cross-account access to a Kinesis stream requires creating a role in the account that owns the resource with the needed stream permissions, plus a trust policy allowing Account A's instance profile role to assume it, after which the application calls AssumeRole to obtain temporary Account B credentials. Adding stream-read permissions directly to the Account A instance role (A) does not grant access to a resource IAM cannot reach in another account, and Kinesis does not support resource-based stream policies the way S3 or Secrets Manager do, so a resource-based policy on the stream (E) is not how this is authorized.

questions.question: An ecommerce startup is preparing for an annual sales event. As the traffic to the company's application increases, the development team wants to be notified when the Amazon EC2 instance's CPU utilization exceeds 80%. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Create a custom Amazon CloudWatch alarm that sends a notification to an Amazon SNS topic when the CPU utilization exceeds 80%.
Create a custom AWS CloudTrail alarm that sends a notification to an Amazon SNS topic when the CPU utilization exceeds 80%.
Create a cron job on the EC2 instance that invokes the --describe-instance-information command on the host instance every 15 minutes and sends the results to an Amazon SNS topic.
Create an AWS Lambda function that queries the AWS CloudTrail logs for the CPUUtilization metric every 15 minutes and sends a notification to an Amazon SNS topic when the CPU utilization exceeds 80%.
questions.explanation: A CloudWatch alarm on the EC2 CPUUtilization metric with an SNS action is the native threshold-notification pattern for the 80% requirement. CloudTrail records API calls rather than emitting CPU metrics or alarms; a cron job polling instance metadata is custom and delayed; Lambda querying CloudTrail logs cannot read live CPU utilization.

questions.question: A company has an application that is deployed on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The application generates user-specific PDFs and stores the PDFs in an Amazon S3 bucket. The application then uses Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) to send the PDFs by email to subscribers. Users no longer access the PDFs 90 days after the PDFs are generated. The S3 bucket is not versioned and contains many obsolete PDFs. A developer must reduce the number of files in the S3 bucket by removing PDFs that are older than 90 days. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST development effort?
options: Update the application code. In the code, add a rule to scan all the objects in the S3 bucket every day and to delete objects after 90 days.
Create an AWS Lambda function. Program the Lambda function to scan all the objects in the S3 bucket every day and to delete objects after 90 days.
Create an S3 Lifecycle rule for the S3 bucket to expire objects after 90 days.
Partition the S3 objects with a / / key prefix. Create an AWS Lambda function to remove objects that have prefixes that have reached the expiration date.
questions.explanation: An S3 Lifecycle rule configured to expire (delete) objects after 90 days is the native, built-in mechanism to automatically remove old PDFs with zero custom code, matching the least development effort. Updating application code to scan and delete objects daily (A) or building a dedicated Lambda function to do the same (B) both reimplement functionality S3 Lifecycle rules already provide natively, and partitioning objects by a key prefix with a custom Lambda cleanup function (D) adds unnecessary restructuring and code compared to a straightforward Lifecycle rule.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting an application. The application includes several AWS Lambda functions that invoke an Amazon API Gateway API. The API Gateway's method request is set up to use an Amazon Cognito authorizer for authentication. All the Lambda functions pass the user ID as part of the Authorization header to the API Gateway API. The API Gateway API returns a 403 status code for all GET requests. How should the developer resolve this issue?
options: Modify the client GET request to include a valid API key in the Authorization header.
Modify the client GET request to include a valid token in the Authorization header.
Update the resource policy for the API Gateway API to allow the execute-api:Invoke action.
Modify the client to send an OPTIONS preflight request before the GET request.
questions.explanation: Since the API uses a Cognito authorizer, the Authorization header must contain a valid Cognito-issued token (a JWT), not an arbitrary user ID string, so sending a plain user ID instead of the token is why every GET request is rejected with 403. An API key (A) is not what a Cognito authorizer validates, updating the resource policy for execute-api:Invoke (C) controls resource-level access rather than per-user token validation, and a CORS preflight request (D) is unrelated to why an authenticated GET call is being rejected.

questions.question: A company processes incoming documents from an Amazon S3 bucket. Users upload documents to an S3 bucket using a web user interface. Upon receiving files in S3, an AWS Lambda function is invoked to process the files, but the Lambda function times out intermittently. If the Lambda function is configured with the default settings, what will happen to the S3 event when there is a timeout exception?
options: Notification of a failed S3 event is sent as an email through Amazon SNS.
The S3 event is sent to the default Dead Letter Queue.
The S3 event is processed until it is successful.
The S3 event is discarded after the event is retried twice.
questions.explanation: With Lambda's default asynchronous invocation configuration, a failed invocation (such as a timeout) is retried up to two additional times, and if all attempts still fail, the event is discarded (unless a destination or dead-letter queue is configured to instead capture it). There is no default Dead Letter Queue configured automatically (B, that must be explicitly set up), an email notification through SNS is not sent automatically by default (A), and the event is not retried indefinitely until success (C), since Lambda's default async retry behavior is bounded at two retries.

questions.question: A developer uses Amazon S3 Event Notifications to invoke AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda functions process images after the images are uploaded to S3 buckets. The developer has set up a development S3 bucket, a production S3 bucket, a development Lambda function, and a production Lambda function in the same AWS account. The developer notices that uploads to the development S3 bucket wrongly invoke the production Lambda function. The developer must prevent development data from affecting the production Lambda function. What should the developer do to meet these requirements?
options: Update the execution role for the production Lambda function. Add a policy that allows the execution role to read from only the production S3 bucket.
Update the S3 bucket policy for the production S3 bucket to invoke the production Lambda function. Update the S3 bucket policy for the development S3 bucket to invoke the development Lambda function.

Separate the development environment and the production environment into their own AWS accounts. Update the execution role for each Lambda function. Add a policy that allows the execution role to read from only the S3 bucket that is in the same account.

Separate the development environment and the production environment into their own AWS accounts. Add a resource policy to the Lambda functions to allow only S3 bucket events in the same account to invoke the functions.
questions.explanation: Separating the development and production environments into their own AWS accounts, combined with a resource policy on each Lambda function that allows invocation only from S3 buckets within the same account, structurally prevents any cross-account (and thus cross-environment) invocation regardless of naming or configuration mistakes, which is the security best practice for this kind of isolation. Restricting only the execution role to read from the production bucket (A) controls what the function can access after being invoked, it does not stop the wrong bucket from invoking it in the first place, and updating S3 bucket policies to specify which Lambda function to invoke (B) does not exist as an S3 bucket policy capability, since S3 event notification targets are configured on the bucket's notification configuration, not enforced through a bucket policy naming a specific function.

questions.question: A developer is writing an application that will run on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The developer wants to externalize the session state to support the application. Which AWS services or resources can the developer use to meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon Cognito
Amazon ElastiCache
Application Load Balancer
Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS)
questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon ElastiCache are both purpose-built, externally hosted data stores well suited to holding session state independently of any single EC2 instance in the Auto Scaling group, letting any instance read or write the same session data. Amazon Cognito (B) manages user identity and authentication rather than arbitrary session state, an Application Load Balancer (D) can provide sticky sessions but does not itself externalize or store session data, and Amazon SQS (E) is a message queue, not a store suited for reading and updating live session state.

questions.question: A company has a serverless application that uses an Amazon API Gateway API to invoke an AWS Lambda function. A developer creates a fix for a defect in the Lambda function code. The developer wants to deploy this fix to the production environment. To test the changes, the developer needs to send 10% of the live production traffic to the updated Lambda function version. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Publish a new version of the Lambda function that contains the updated code.
Set up a new stage in API Gateway with a new Lambda function version. Enable weighted routing in API Gateway stages.
Create an alias for the Lambda function. Configure weighted routing on the alias. Specify a 10% weight for the new Lambda function version.
Set up a routing policy on a Network Load Balancer. Configure 10% of the traffic to go to the new Lambda function version.
Set up a weighted routing policy by using Amazon Route 53. Configure 10% of the traffic to go to the new Lambda function version.
questions.explanation: Publishing a new version of the Lambda function with the fixed code, then creating an alias with weighted routing that sends 10% of invocations to that new version while the rest continue to the existing version, is Lambda's native, built-in canary-testing mechanism requiring no additional infrastructure. Introducing a new API Gateway stage with its own weighted routing (B) is not how traffic-splitting works for Lambda versions, since alias-level weighting already handles this, and routing through a Network Load Balancer or Amazon Route 53 weighted policy (D, E) both introduce infrastructure not needed when Lambda aliases natively support weighted routing between versions.

questions.question: A developer is creating a video search application for a global company. The video files have an average size of 2.5 TB. The video storage system must provide instant access to the video files for the first 90 days. After the first 90 days, the video files can take more than 10 minutes to load. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Upload the video files to the Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) Standard storage class for the first 90 days. After 90 days, transition the video files to the EFS Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) storage class.
Upload the video files to Amazon S3. Use the S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class for the first 90 days. After 90 days, transition the video file to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class.
Use Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) to store the video files for the first 90 days. After 90 days, transition the video files to the Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class.

Upload the video files to Amazon S3. Use the S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage class for the first 90 days. After 90 days, transition the video files to the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class.
questions.explanation: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval provides instant (millisecond) access to the video files for the first 90 days at a lower cost than S3 Standard for infrequently accessed large files, and transitioning to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval afterward, when access can tolerate more than 10 minutes, further reduces storage cost for data accessed less often. S3 Glacier Deep Archive (B) has retrieval times measured in hours, far exceeding the 'instant access' requirement for the first 90 days, EFS (A) is a file system service with higher per-GB cost than S3 for this kind of large, infrequently modified video archive, and EBS with manual Glacier transitions via snapshots (C) is a more complex, less directly applicable pattern than S3's own native storage class transitions for object data.

questions.question: A company has an ecommerce platform. A developer is designing an Amazon DynamoDB table to store customer order data for the platform. The table uses the order ID as the partition key. The developer needs to modify the table to get all order IDs that are associated with a given customer email address in a single query. The solution must give the developer the ability to query order IDs by other item attributes in the future. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the partition key to use the customer email address as the sort key.
Update the table to use the customer email address as the partition key.
Create a local secondary index (LSI) with the customer email address as the sort key.
Create a global secondary index (GSI) with the customer email address as the partition key.
questions.explanation: Adding a GSI with the customer email address as its partition key lets the application efficiently query all order IDs for a given email in a single request, and because a GSI can later be extended or complemented by additional GSIs, the developer retains the ability to query by other attributes in the future without restructuring the base table. Making the email address the sort key of the existing primary key (A) does not let you query across all orders for an email independently of the order ID partition key, changing the base table's partition key entirely (B) is a disruptive restructuring, and an LSI (C) must share the base table's existing partition key (order ID), so it cannot be keyed independently by email address.

questions.question: A company has a virtual reality (VR) game. The game has a serverless backend that consists of Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, and Amazon DynamoDB. Recently, the company noticed a sudden increase of new users globally. The company also noticed delays in the retrieval of user data. Which AWS service or feature can the company use to reduce the database response time to microseconds?
options: Amazon ElastiCache
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DynamoDB auto scaling
Amazon CloudFront
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory caching layer purpose-built to sit in front of DynamoDB and reduce read response times from single-digit milliseconds down to microseconds, directly addressing the described latency issue for a growing global user base. Amazon ElastiCache (A) would require the application to manage its own cache-aside logic against DynamoDB rather than using DynamoDB's own purpose-built accelerator, DynamoDB auto scaling (C) adjusts capacity over time to match sustained load but does not itself reduce per-request latency to microseconds, and CloudFront (D) accelerates content delivery for cacheable web content, it is not a database response-time accelerator.

questions.question: A developer is creating a solution to track an account's Amazon S3 buckets over time. The developer has created an AWS Lambda function that will run on a schedule. The function will list the account's S3 buckets and will store the list in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The developer receives a permissions error when the developer runs the function with the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole AWS managed policy. Which combination of permissions should the developer use to resolve this error? (Choose two.)
options: Cross-account IAM role
Permission for the Lambda function to list buckets in Amazon S3
Permission for the Lambda function to write in DynamoDB
Permission for Amazon S3 to invoke the Lambda function
Permission for DynamoDB to invoke the Lambda function
questions.explanation: Since AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole only grants CloudWatch Logs permissions, the function additionally needs explicit permission to call s3:ListBucket (to enumerate the account's S3 buckets) and permission to write items into the DynamoDB table, which are the two missing capabilities causing the observed permissions error. Cross-account IAM roles (A) are unnecessary for a function that only needs to read within its own account's S3 buckets and write to its own DynamoDB table, and Amazon S3 or DynamoDB do not need permission to 'invoke' the Lambda function (D, E) here, since the function runs on a schedule rather than being invoked by either of those services.

questions.question: A company uses AWS to run its learning management system (LMS) application. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application's domain name is managed in Amazon Route 53. The application is deployed in a single AWS Region, but the company wants to improve application performance for users all over the world. Which solution will improve global performance with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the ALB as the origin server. Configure Route 53 to create a DNS alias record that points the application's domain name to the CloudFront distribution URL.
Launch more EC2 instances behind the ALConfigure the ALB to use session affinity (sticky sessions). Create a Route 53 alias record for the ALB by using a geolocation routing policy.

Create an AWS Client VPN endpoint in the VPInstruct users to connect to the VPN to access the application. Create a Route 53 alias record for the VPN endpoint. Configure Route 53 to use a geolocation routing policy.
Deploy the application to multiple Regions across the world. Create a Route 53 alias record for the ALB by using a latency-based routing policy.
questions.explanation: Setting up a CloudFront distribution with the existing ALB as its origin, then adding a Route 53 alias record pointing the application's domain to the CloudFront distribution, lets CloudFront's global edge network cache and accelerate content delivery to users worldwide, all with a single managed distribution and no application redeployment. Enabling sticky sessions and geolocation routing to more instances behind the same single-Region ALB (B) does not improve performance for users physically far from that one Region, a Client VPN endpoint (C) is meant for private connectivity rather than public global performance, and deploying to multiple Regions with latency-based routing (D) achieves similar goals but requires far more operational overhead (multi-Region deployment and data synchronization) than adding a CloudFront distribution in front of the existing single-Region deployment.

questions.question: A developer hosts a static website on Amazon S3 and connects the website to an Amazon CloudFront distribution. The website uses a custom domain name that points to the CloudFront URL. The developer has set up a continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline. The pipeline automatically runs when changes occur in an AWS CodeCommit repository. The pipeline has a source stage and then a build stage. The build stage invokes an AWS CodeBuild project that references a buildspec.yml file. The buildspec.yml file builds the code and deploys the static files to the S3 bucket. The pipeline runs successfully, and the latest website files are visible in the S3 bucket and at the S3 website URL. However, when the developer accesses the website through the CloudFront domain, the updates are not reflected on the website. What should the developer configure the buildspec.yml file to do to resolve this issue?
options: Properly synchronize the objects in the S3 bucket with new files from the source stage.
Delete the previous website files in the S3 bucket and redeploy the website files.
Invalidate the file caches for the primary CloudFront distribution.
Modify the cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) policy of the S3 bucket and redeploy the website files.
questions.explanation: CloudFront caches origin content at edge locations for the duration of its TTL settings, so even after the S3 bucket's files are updated, CloudFront can continue serving the previously cached (stale) version until an invalidation is issued for those file paths, which is exactly why the S3 URL shows updates immediately but the CloudFront domain does not. Re-syncing objects in the S3 bucket differently (A) does not address CloudFront's own edge cache, since the S3 content is already correctly updated, deleting and redeploying the same files (B) does not itself force CloudFront to bypass its cache either, and a CORS policy change (D) addresses cross-origin browser access rules, it has nothing to do with CloudFront serving stale cached content.

questions.question: A developer is working on an ecommerce application that stores data in an Amazon RDS for MySQL cluster. The developer needs to implement a caching layer for the application to retrieve information about the most viewed products. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Edit the RDS for MySQL cluster by adding a cache node. Configure the cache endpoint instead of the cluster endpoint in the application.
Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster. Update the application code to use the ElastiCache for Redis cluster endpoint.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the RDS for MySQL cluster. Configure the application to connect to the DAX endpoint instead of the RDS endpoint.
Configure the RDS for MySQL cluster to add a standby instance in a different Availability Zone. Configure the application to read the data from the standby instance.
questions.explanation: Creating an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster and updating the application to read/write through its endpoint adds a purpose-built, flexible in-memory caching layer in front of RDS for MySQL to serve frequently requested product information with low latency. RDS does not support attaching a 'cache node' directly to a cluster the way described (A), a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster only works in front of DynamoDB tables, not an RDS for MySQL cluster (C), and adding a standby instance for reads (D) is not how RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ works, since the standby is for failover and is not readable in the standard MySQL Multi-AZ configuration.

questions.question: A developer is creating a database of products. Queries for frequently accessed products must have retrieval times of microseconds. To ensure data consistency, the application cache must be updated whenever products are added, changed, or deleted. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Set up an Amazon DynamoDB database and a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster.
Set up an Amazon RDS database and an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster. Implement a lazy loading caching strategy with ElastiCache.
Setup an Amazon DynamoDB database that has an in-memory cache. Implement a lazy loading caching strategy in the application.
Set up an Amazon RDS database and an Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster. Specify a TTL setting for the DAX cluster.
questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB paired with a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster is purpose-built to deliver microsecond retrieval times for frequently accessed items, and DAX automatically keeps the cache consistent by writing through to DynamoDB (and updating the cache) whenever items are added, changed, or deleted through the DAX client, satisfying the consistency requirement natively. RDS paired with ElastiCache using lazy loading (B) can serve stale cached data until the next cache miss refreshes it, an 'in-memory cache' built into DynamoDB without DAX (C) does not exist as a distinct DynamoDB feature, and pairing RDS with DAX (D) is not valid since DAX only works with DynamoDB tables, not RDS.

questions.question: A developer is creating a script to automate the deployment process for a serverless application. The developer wants to use an existing AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) template for the application. What should the developer use for the project? (Choose two.)
options: Call aws cloudformation package to create the deployment package. Call aws cloudformation deploy to deploy the package afterward.
Call sam package to create the deployment package. Call sam deploy to deploy the package afterward.
Call aws s3 cp to upload the AWS SAM template to Amazon S3. Call aws lambda update-function-code to create the application.
Create a ZIP package locally and call aws serverlessrepo create-applicatiion to create the application.
Create a ZIP package and upload it to Amazon S3. Call aws cloudformation create-stack to create the application.
questions.explanation: Using the sam package and sam deploy commands is the SAM CLI's own purpose-built workflow for taking an existing AWS SAM template, packaging its local code assets to S3, and deploying the resulting CloudFormation stack, and because a SAM template is fundamentally a CloudFormation template with a Transform, manually zipping the code, uploading it to S3, and then calling aws cloudformation create-stack directly against the SAM template (with the code already staged at the referenced S3 location) is also a technically valid, if more manual, way to deploy it. Manually uploading the SAM template itself to S3 and separately calling aws lambda update-function-code (C) does not actually deploy the described infrastructure via CloudFormation at all, and treating a locally zipped package as an 'application' to register via aws serverlessrepo create-application (D) is for publishing to the AWS Serverless Application Repository, not for deploying the application's own infrastructure stack.

questions.question: A developer adds new dependencies to an existing AWS Lambda function. The developer cannot deploy the Lambda function because the unzipped deployment package exceeds the maximum size quota for the Lambda function. The instruction set architecture of the Lambda function is x86_64. The developer must implement a solution to deploy the Lambda function with the new dependencies. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a snapshot of all the dependencies. Configure the Lambda function to use the snapshot.
Change the instruction set architecture of the Lambda function to use an arm64 architecture.
Associate an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume with the Lambda function. Store all the dependencies on the EBS volume.
Create and deploy a Lambda container image with all the dependencies.
questions.explanation: Creating and deploying a Lambda function packaged as a container image raises the effective size limit dramatically (container images support up to 10 GB, compared to the .zip deployment package's 250 MB unzipped limit), directly resolving a deployment package that has exceeded the standard size quota. Creating a 'snapshot of dependencies' (A) is not a real Lambda deployment mechanism, switching the instruction set architecture to arm64 (B) changes the underlying processor architecture and has no bearing on the maximum allowed package size, and attaching an EBS volume to a Lambda function (C) is not supported, since Lambda functions cannot have EBS volumes attached to them directly.

questions.question: A developer is working on a project that requires regular updates to a web application’s backend code. The code is stored in AWS CodeCommit. Company policy states that all code must have complete unit testing and that the test results must be available for access. The developer needs to implement a solution that will take each change to the code repository, build the code, and run unit tests. The solution also must provide a detailed report of the test results. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure AWS CodeDeploy to deploy code from CodeCommit and to run unit tests. Send the test results to Amazon CloudWatch metrics to view reports.
Configure Amazon CodeWhisperer to create the code and to run unit tests. Save the test results in an Amazon S3 bucket to generate reports.
Configure AWS CodeBuild to build the code and to run unit tests. Use test reporting in CodeBuild to generate and view reports.
Create AWS Lambda functions that run when changes are made in CodeCommit. Program the Lambda functions to build the code, run unit tests, and save the test results to a Lambda layer.
questions.explanation: Configuring AWS CodeBuild to build the code and run unit tests, using CodeBuild's built-in test reporting feature (configured through the buildspec's reports section), triggers on every change through the CI/CD pipeline and produces a detailed, accessible report of the test results natively, with no extra service needed. AWS CodeDeploy (A) automates deployments rather than running unit tests or generating test reports, Amazon CodeWhisperer (B) is an AI coding assistant, not a build/test execution or reporting tool, and building custom Lambda functions to run tests and save results to a Lambda layer (D) reimplements build/test/report functionality that CodeBuild's native test reports feature already provides, and Lambda layers are meant for shared code, not for storing test result data.

questions.question: A developer is building an application on AWS. The application has an Amazon API Gateway API that sends requests to an AWS Lambda function. The API is experiencing increased latency because the Lambda function has limited available CPU to fulfill the requests. Before the developer deploys the API into production, the developer must configure the Lambda function to have more CPU. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Increase the virtual CPU (vCPU) cores quota of the Lambda function.
Increase the amount of memory that is allocated to the Lambda function.
Increase the ephemeral storage size of the Lambda function.
Increase the timeout value of the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Increasing the memory allocated to the Lambda function proportionally increases the amount of CPU power available to it, since Lambda allocates vCPU in proportion to configured memory, directly giving the function more compute to work with. There is no separate 'vCPU core quota' setting to increase directly on a Lambda function (A), increasing ephemeral storage (C) only affects /tmp disk space, not CPU, and increasing the timeout value (D) only changes how long the function is allowed to run, it does not give it more CPU.

questions.question: A developer is creating a web application to upload and store private data. The application will encrypt private data and then will upload the data to an Amazon S3 bucket. The developer needs to implement a solution to automatically find any unencrypted private data in the S3 bucket.
