The solution must monitor the security and access control of the S3 bucket and must provide a notification if there are any security issues. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Step Functions to run Amazon Athena queries. Configure Athena to find unencrypted private data and to monitor for security issues in the S3 bucket. Start the queries when new objects are added to the S3 bucket. Configure Athena to provide a notification if security issues are detected.

Enable Amazon Macie for the S3 bucket. Set up custom criteria to find unencrypted private data in the S3 bucket. Set up AWS User Notifications to provide a notification when Macie detects security issues.

Enable Amazon Inspector for the AWS account. Use Amazon Inspector to scan the S3 bucket to find unencrypted private data and to monitor for security issues. Set up Amazon EventBridge to provide a notification when Amazon Inspector detects security issues.

Create an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Configure Amazon S3 to send new object notifications to the stream. Create an AWS Lambda function that runs every 10 minutes to check the stream for unencrypted private data and to monitor for security issues. Program the Lambda function to provide a notification when security issues are detected.
questions.explanation: Enabling Amazon Macie for the S3 bucket, with custom criteria configured to detect unencrypted private data, combined with AWS User Notifications to alert on Macie findings, is a managed, purpose-built service for exactly this kind of sensitive-data-and-security-posture monitoring with built-in notification integration. Using Step Functions to run ad hoc Athena queries (A) requires building custom detection logic that Macie already provides natively, Amazon Inspector (C) is designed for vulnerability scanning of compute resources like EC2 and container images, not S3 data content or bucket access-control posture, and a custom Lambda function polling a Kinesis stream every 10 minutes (D) reimplements sensitive-data detection logic that Macie is purpose-built to perform.

questions.question: A developer has an application that uses AWS Lambda functions and AWS CloudFormation templates. Usage of the application has increased. As a result, the Lambda functions are encountering rate limit errors when they retrieve data. The Lambda functions retrieve an advanced parameter from AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store on every call. The parameter changes only during new deployments. Because the application’s usage is unpredictable, the developer needs a way to avoid the rate limiting. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Configure the Lambda functions to use reserved concurrency that is equal to the last month’s average number of concurrent invocations.
Add a retry mechanism with exponential backoff to the call to Parameter Store.
Request a service quota increase for Parameter Store GetParameter API operations to match the expected usage of the Lambda functions.
Add an SSM dynamic reference as an environment variable to the Lambda functions resource in the CloudFormation templates.
questions.explanation: Adding an SSM dynamic reference to the Lambda function's environment variable in the CloudFormation template resolves the Parameter Store value at deployment/update time and bakes it into the function configuration, so the Lambda function no longer needs to call Parameter Store's GetParameter API on every invocation, eliminating the rate-limiting calls entirely at effectively no extra cost. Reserved concurrency based on last month's average (A) does not address the underlying cause of repeated GetParameter calls, adding retry with backoff (B) only reduces failed-call impact rather than the call volume itself, and requesting a service quota increase (C) is more costly and less clean than simply avoiding the repeated calls altogether via a dynamic reference resolved at deploy time.

questions.question: A developer is using an AWS Lambda function to process data. The developer needs to extract custom metrics about processing times from the Lambda logs. The developer needs to analyze the metrics, set alarms, and detect issues in real time. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Publish custom metric data to AWS CloudTrail by using the PutMetricData API operation. Classify and collect the metrics. Create graphs and alarms in CloudTrail for the custom metrics.

Use the open source client libraries provided by Amazon to generate the logs in the Amazon CloudWatch embedded metric format. Use CloudWatch to create the required graphs and alarms for the custom metrics.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to create custom metrics by querying the logs that come from the Lambda function. Use CloudWatch to create the required graphs and alarms for the custom metrics.

Create an Amazon Kinesis data stream to stream log events in real time from Lambda. Specify an Amazon S3 bucket as the destination for the Kinesis data stream. Use Amazon CloudWatch to visualize the log data and to set alarms.
questions.explanation: The CloudWatch embedded metric format lets Lambda log lines carry metric values that CloudWatch extracts automatically for graphing, alarming, and real-time detection. CloudTrail does not host custom application metrics; Logs Insights queries are ad hoc rather than continuous metric extraction; Kinesis to S3 archives logs instead of producing CloudWatch metrics.

questions.question: A developer needs to fix an AWS CodeDeploy deployment that failed. During the failed deployment, the developer received the following error message: “The overall deployment failed because too many individual instances failed deployment, too few healthy instances are available for deployment, or some instances in your deployment group are experiencing problems. (Error code: HEALTH-CONSTRAINTS)” What are the possible causes of the failed deployment? (Choose two.)
options: The CodeDeploy agent was not running on the instances that CodeDeploy was trying to deploy to.
The unified Amazon CloudWatch agent was not running on the instances that CodeDeploy was trying to deploy to.
The developer’s IAM role did not have the necessary permissions to perform code deployment to the instances.
CodeDeploy was trying to deploy to instances that were attached to an IAM instance profile that did not have the required permissions.
CodeDeploy was trying to deploy to instances that were not set up with correct CodeDeploy health checks.
questions.explanation: A HEALTH-CONSTRAINTS error in CodeDeploy is caused either by the CodeDeploy agent not actually running on the target instances (so the deployment cannot execute lifecycle hooks and report health) or by the deployment group's health checks or configuration not being properly set up to reflect instance health accurately, both of which directly explain CodeDeploy reporting too many unhealthy or unreachable instances. The CloudWatch agent (B) is unrelated to CodeDeploy's own health reporting mechanism, and while an IAM role or instance profile lacking the right permissions (C, D) would cause deployment permission errors, those surface as distinctly different error types (typically authorization failures) rather than the HEALTH-CONSTRAINTS error described here.

questions.question: A company is developing a serverless application that requires storage of sensitive API keys as environment variables for various services. The application requires the automatic rotation of the encryption keys every year. Which solution will meet these requirements with no development effort?
options: Encrypt the environment variables by using AWS Secrets Manager. Set up automatic rotation in Secrets Manager.
Encrypt the environment variables by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed keys. Enable automatic key rotation.
Encrypt the environment variables by using AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) AWS managed keys. Configure a custom AWS Lambda function to automate key rotation.
Encrypt the environment variables by using AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Set up automatic rotation in Parameter Store.
questions.explanation: KMS customer managed keys support enabling automatic annual key rotation with a single setting and no code, directly meeting 'no development effort' for rotating the encryption key used on the environment variables. Secrets Manager rotation (A) rotates the secret's value rather than the encryption key, AWS managed keys (C) do not offer customer-controlled rotation scheduling, and Parameter Store (D) manages parameter values, not KMS key rotation.

questions.question: An application stores user data in Amazon S3 buckets in multiple AWS Regions. A developer needs to implement a solution that analyzes the user data in the S3 buckets to find sensitive information. The analysis findings from all the S3 buckets must be available in the eu-west-2 Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
options: Create an AWS Lambda function to generate findings. Program the Lambda function to send the findings to another S3 bucket in eu-west-2.
Configure Amazon Macie to generate findings. Use Amazon EventBridge to create rules that copy the findings to eu-west-2.
Configure Amazon Inspector to generate findings. Use Amazon EventBridge to create rules that copy the findings to eu-west-2.
Configure Amazon Macie to generate findings and to publish the findings to AWS CloudTrail. Use a CloudTrail trail to copy the results to eu-west-2.
questions.explanation: Amazon Macie natively scans S3 buckets across Regions to detect sensitive data, and pairing it with Amazon EventBridge rules that copy Macie's findings to the eu-west-2 Region centralizes results with minimal custom development, since both the detection and the cross-Region distribution use managed AWS services. A custom Lambda function to generate findings (A) reimplements what Macie already provides as a managed capability, and Amazon Inspector (C) scans compute resources for vulnerabilities rather than S3 object content for sensitive data, so it does not fit this requirement, while publishing findings through CloudTrail (D) is not how Macie findings are natively distributed; Macie integrates with EventBridge for that purpose.

questions.question: An application ingests data from an Amazon Kinesis data stream. The shards in the data stream are set for normal traffic. During tests for peak traffic, the application ingests data slowly. A developer needs to adjust the data stream to handle the peak traffic. What should the developer do to meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?
options: Install the Kinesis Producer Library (KPL) to ingest data into the data stream.
Switch to on-demand capacity mode for the data stream. Specify a partition key when writing data to the data stream.
Decrease the amount of time that data is kept in the data stream by using the DecreaseStreamRetentionPeriod API operation.
Increase the shard count in the data stream by using the UpdateShardCount API operation.
questions.explanation: Increasing the Kinesis data stream's shard count using the UpdateShardCount API operation directly increases the stream's read/write throughput capacity to handle the peak traffic, at a cost proportional only to the additional shards actually needed. Installing the Kinesis Producer Library (A) can improve producer-side efficiency but does not itself increase the stream's provisioned shard capacity, decreasing the retention period (C) reduces how long data is stored, it does not increase ingestion throughput, and switching to on-demand mode (B) is also a valid alternative, but increasing shard count in provisioned mode is the more directly cost-controlled adjustment matching the existing 'normal traffic' provisioned setup described.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that uses an AWS Lambda function to process data. The application requires minimum latency. The Lambda function must have predictable function start times. All setup activities for the execution environment must happen before invocation of the Lambda function. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Increase the memory of the Lambda function to the maximum amount. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to schedule invocations of the Lambda function every minute to keep the execution environment active.

Optimize the static initialization code that runs when a new execution environment is prepared for the first time. Decrease and compress the size of the Lambda function package and the imported libraries and dependencies.

Increase the reserved concurrency of the Lambda function to the maximum value for unreserved account concurrency. Run any setup activities manually before the initial invocation of the Lambda function.
Publish a new version of the Lambda function. Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function with the required minimum number of execution environments.
questions.explanation: Provisioned concurrency on a published version pre-initializes the requested number of execution environments, so setup completes before invocation and start times stay predictable with minimum latency. Scheduled pings only reduce cold starts opportunistically; code and package optimization helps but cannot guarantee pre-initialized capacity; reserved concurrency limits throughput rather than pre-warming environments.

questions.question: A company has implemented a pipeline in AWS CodePipeline. The company is using a single AWS account and does not use AWS Organizations. The company needs to test its AWS CloudFormation templates in its primary AWS Region and a disaster recovery Region. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: In the CodePipeline pipeline, implement an AWS CodeDeploy action for each Region to deploy and test the CloudFormation templates. Update CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild with appropriate permissions.
Configure CodePipeline to deploy and test the CloudFormation templates. Use CloudFormation StackSets to start deployment across both Regions.
Configure CodePipeline to invoke AWS CodeBuild to deploy and test the CloudFormation templates in each Region. Update CodeBuild and CloudFormation with appropriate permissions.
Use the Snyk action in CodePipeline to deploy and test the CloudFormation templates in each Region.
questions.explanation: CloudFormation StackSets natively support deploying the same CloudFormation template consistently across multiple Regions from a single CodePipeline stage, avoiding the need to build and manage separate per-Region deployment actions or permissions configurations. Adding a separate CodeDeploy action per Region (A) does not use CloudFormation's native multi-Region deployment capability at all, invoking CodeBuild per Region to run CloudFormation commands manually (C) reimplements what StackSets already automates, and using an unrelated third-party 'Snyk action' (D) is a security-scanning integration, not a mechanism for deploying CloudFormation templates across Regions.

questions.question: A company has an Amazon API Gateway REST API that integrates with an AWS Lambda function. The API’s development stage references a development alias of the Lambda function named dev. A developer needs make a production alias of the Lambda function named prod available through the API. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Create a new method on the API. Name the method production. Configure the method to include a stage variable that points to the prod Lambda function alias.
Create a new method on the API. Name the method production. Configure an integration request on the API’s development stage that points to the prod Lambda function alias.
Deploy the API to a new stage named production. Configure the stage to include a stage variable that points to the prod Lambda function alias.
Deploy the API to a new stage named production. Configure an integration request on the API’s production stage that points to the prod Lambda function alias.
questions.explanation: Deploying the API to a brand-new stage named production, with an integration request configured on that production stage to reference the Lambda function's prod alias, cleanly separates the production traffic path (and its own stage-specific configuration) from the existing development stage, which continues to reference the dev alias unaffected. Adding a new method (rather than a new stage) named 'production' (A, B) does not create the isolated deployment stage needed to serve a distinct environment, and configuring a stage variable rather than directly setting the integration request's target (A, C) does not match the described requirement to have the production stage's own integration point at the prod alias directly.

questions.question: A developer is implementing a serverless application by using AWS CloudFormation to provision Amazon S3 web hosting. Amazon API Gateway, and AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda function source code is zipped and uploaded to an S3 bucket. The S3 object key of the zipped source code is specified in the Lambda resource in the CloudFormation template. The developer notices that there are no changes in the Lambda function every time the CloudFormation stack is updated. How can the developer resolve this issue?
options: Create a new Lambda function alias before updating the CloudFormation stack.
Change the S3 object key or the S3 version in the CloudFormation template before updating the CloudFormation stack.
Upload the zipped source code to another S3 bucket before updating the CioudFormation stack.
Associate a cade signing configuration with the Lambda function before updating the CloudFormation stack.
questions.explanation: CloudFormation only updates an AWS::Lambda::Function resource's code when it detects a change to the resource's own properties, so simply re-uploading a new .zip file to the same S3 key (with the S3Bucket and S3Key values in the template left unchanged) does not register as a template change; updating the S3 object key (or specifying a new S3 object version) so the template's referenced value actually changes forces CloudFormation to update the function. Creating a new function alias (A) does not affect which code version the underlying function resource points to, uploading to an entirely different bucket without also updating the template's reference to it (C) still leaves the template pointing at the old, unchanged key, and adding a code-signing configuration (D) is unrelated to whether CloudFormation detects a code change to redeploy.

questions.question: A developer published a change to a new version of an AWS Lambda function. To test the change, the developer must route 50% of the traffic to the new version and 60% of the traffic to the current version. What is the MOST operationally efficient way to meet this requirement?
options: Create two Amazon Route 53 records that use a simple routing policy to route traffic to the different versions of the Lambda function. Create another Route 53 record that uses a weighted routing policy to route 50% of the traffic to each simple routing record. Test the Lambda function by using the weighted routing record.

Create an Amazon API Gateway API with a POST method that is integrated with the Lambda function. Add a stage variable that includes the version of the Lambda function. Add a canary release that will override the version variable 50% of the time. Deploy and test the Lambda function through the API Gateway stage.
Create a Lambda function alias. Set the weight to 50% for the current version and 50% for the new version. Set the event source mappings for the Lambda function to point to the alias.
Update the event source mappings for the Lambda function. In the mappings, set the weight to 50% for the current version and 50% for the new version.
questions.explanation: Creating a Lambda function alias with its weight set to 50% for the current version and 50% for the new version is Lambda's native, purpose-built mechanism for splitting invocation traffic between two versions by percentage, requiring no additional AWS services and matching the requirement with the least operational overhead. Using Route 53 weighted DNS records (A) or an API Gateway canary release with a stage variable override (B) both introduce extra routing layers on top of what a Lambda weighted alias already does directly, and Lambda event source mappings (D) configure how events are pulled from a source like SQS, they have no 'weight' setting for splitting traffic between function versions.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that processes a stream of user-supplied data. The data stream must be consumed by multiple Amazon EC2 based processing applications in parallel and in real time. Each processor must be able to resume without losing data if there is a service interruption. The application architect plans to add other processors in the near future, and wants to minimize the amount of data duplication involved. Which solution will satisfy these requirements?
options: Publish the data to Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS).
Publish the data to Amazon Data Firehose.
Publish the data to Amazon EventBridge.
Publish the data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.
questions.explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams natively supports multiple independent consumer applications reading the same stream concurrently in real time, and each consumer's position (checkpoint) in the stream lets it resume exactly where it left off after an interruption with no data loss, while adding future consumers requires no duplication of the underlying data. Amazon SQS (A) is designed around a message typically being consumed and removed by one consumer at a time rather than replayed by many independent processors, Kinesis Data Firehose (B) is built for batched delivery to storage/analytics destinations rather than direct real-time processing by multiple custom consumers, and EventBridge (C) is an event-routing service rather than a durable, replayable stream designed for this kind of multi-consumer real-time processing pattern.

questions.question: An application is experiencing performance issues based on increased demand. This increased demand is on read-only historical records pulled from an Amazon RDS-hosted database with custom views and queries. A developer must improve performance without changing the database structure. Which approach will improve performance and MINIMIZE management overhead?
options: Deploy Amazon DynamoDB, move all the data, and point to DynamoDB.
Deploy Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) and cache the data for the application.
Deploy Memcached on Amazon EC2 and cache the data for the application.
Deploy Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) on Amazon RDS to improve cache performance.
questions.explanation: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis OSS added in front of the application, caching the results of the read-only historical queries, offloads repeated read traffic from RDS without requiring any changes to the underlying database structure, with lower management overhead than running and maintaining a separate self-managed cache. Migrating all the data into DynamoDB (A) is a much larger architectural change than simply adding a cache layer, running Memcached on a self-managed EC2 instance (C) requires more manual infrastructure management than a managed ElastiCache cluster, and DynamoDB Accelerator (D) only works in front of DynamoDB tables, not an RDS-hosted database.

questions.question: A developer is using AWS CloudFormation to deploy an AWS Lambda function. The developer needs to set the Lambda function's timeout value based on the environment parameter of the template. The template contains mappings of EnvironmentData for each environment's timeout value. The environment parameter and EnvironmentData mappings are as follows: Environment parameter: EnvironmentData mappings: Which statement will meet these requirements?
options: Timeout: !GetAtt [EnvironmentData, !Ref Environment, Timeout]
Timeout: !FindInMap [EnvironmentData, !Ref Environment, Timeout]
Timeout: !Select [EnvironmentData, !Ref Environment, Timeout]
Timeout: !ForEach[EnvironmentData, !Ref Environment, Timeout]
questions.explanation: The Fn::FindInMap intrinsic function looks up a value from the template's Mappings section using the specified top-level key (here, EnvironmentData), a second-level key (the referenced Environment parameter), and the specific attribute name (Timeout), which is exactly the intended way to select an environment-specific value from a CloudFormation mapping. Fn::GetAtt (A) retrieves an attribute of a declared resource, not a value from a Mappings table, Fn::Select (C) picks an item from a list by index, it is not used to navigate a Mappings structure, and Fn::ForEach (D) is used to iterate and generate multiple resources or outputs from a list, it is not a lookup function for retrieving a single mapped value.

questions.question: A company’s AWS accounts are in an organization in AWS Organizations. An application in Account A uses environment variables that are stored as parameters in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. A developer is creating a new application in Account B that needs to use the same environment variables. The application in Account B needs access to the parameters in Account A without duplicating the parameters into Account B. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure the application in Account B to use credentials for an IAM user in AccountA that has access to the parameters.
Create an assumable IAM role in Account A. Grant the role the permission to access the parameters.
Configure cross-account resource sharing for the parameters by using AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
Write a script that stores the parameter values in a private Amazon S3 bucket that both accounts can access.
questions.explanation: The application in Account B can assume a role created in Account A that is scoped to read the specific parameters, using standard STS cross-account role assumption, the lowest-overhead solution that avoids duplicating any parameter. Using IAM user credentials from Account A (A) means managing and sharing long-lived credentials, AWS RAM support for sharing individual Parameter Store parameters across accounts was only introduced later, in February 2024 (C), and syncing values into a shared S3 bucket (D) recreates the duplication the requirement explicitly rules out.

questions.question: In a move toward using microservices, a company’s management team has asked all development teams to build their services so that API requests depend only on that service’s data store. One team is building a Payments service which has its own database; the service needs data that originates in the Accounts database. Both are using Amazon DynamoDB. What approach will result in the simplest, decoupled, and reliable method to get near-real time updates from the Accounts database?
options: Use AWS Glue to perform frequent ETL updates from the Accounts database to the Payments database.
Use Amazon ElastiCache in Payments, with the cache updated by triggers in the Accounts database.
Use Amazon Data Firehose to deliver all changes from the Accounts database to the Payments database.
Use Amazon DynamoDB Streams to deliver all changes from the Accounts database to the Payments database.
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Streams captures every change made to the Accounts table and can directly drive processing (for example, via a Lambda function) that propagates those changes into the Payments database, providing a simple, decoupled, near-real-time replication mechanism without either service directly querying the other's data store. AWS Glue-based ETL (A) is designed for scheduled batch data movement, not near-real-time updates, ElastiCache with database triggers (B) requires building and maintaining custom trigger-and-cache logic, and Kinesis Data Firehose (C) is meant for batched delivery to storage/analytics destinations, not a documented DynamoDB-to-DynamoDB near-real-time replication mechanism the way Streams is.

questions.question: A developer compiles an AWS Lambda function and packages the result as a .zip file. The developer uses the Functions page on the Lambda console to attempt to upload the local packaged .zip file. When pushing the package ta Lambda, the console returns the following error: Which solutions can the developer use to publish the code? (Choose two.)
options: Upload the package to Amazon 3. Use the Functions page on the Lambda console to upload the package from the S3 location.
Create an AWS Support ticket to increase the maximum package size.
Use the update-function-code AWS CLI command. Pass the --publish parameter.

Repackage the Lambda function as a Docker container image. Upload the image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Create a new Lambda function by using the Lambda console. Reference the image that is deployed to Amazon ECR.

Sign the .zip file digitally. Create a new Lambda function by using the Lambda console. Update the configuration of the new Lambda function to include the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the code signing configuration.
questions.explanation: Uploading the oversized package to Amazon S3 first and then using the Lambda console's option to deploy from that S3 location bypasses the console's direct upload size limit (which is much smaller than what a Lambda function can actually run, since S3-sourced .zip deployments support up to 250 MB unzipped), and repackaging the function as a container image uploaded to ECR raises the effective size limit even further (up to 10 GB), both of which are documented ways to work around the console's direct-upload package size restriction. Filing an AWS Support ticket to raise the maximum package size (B) is not possible since Lambda's package size limits are fixed platform quotas rather than adjustable service quotas, using --publish with update-function-code (C) only affects whether a new version is published, it does not change what package size can be uploaded, and digitally signing the .zip file with a code-signing configuration (E) addresses code integrity verification, not the package size limit causing the error.

questions.question: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The application experiences variable loads throughout each day. The company needs to collect detailed metrics from the EC2 instances to right-size the instances. The company also wants to monitor custom application metrics to ensure the application is performing efficiently. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Install the AWS X-Ray agent on the instances. Configure the agent to collect the EC2 instance metrics and the custom application metrics.
Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the instances. Configure the agent to collect the EC2 instance metrics and the custom application metrics.
Install the AWS SDK in the application’s cade. Update the application to use the AWS SDK to collect and publish the EC2 instance metrics and the custom application metrics.
Configure AWS CloudTrail to capture and analyze the EC2 instance metrics and the custom application metrics.
questions.explanation: The CloudWatch agent collects OS-level details such as memory and disk plus custom StatsD or collectd application metrics from Auto Scaling instances, which is exactly what right-sizing and efficiency monitoring need. The X-Ray agent forwards traces rather than host metrics; hand-rolled SDK publishing duplicates agent functionality; CloudTrail audits API calls rather than instance performance.

questions.question: A developer is creating an application that uses an Amazon DynamoDB table. The developer needs to develop code that reads all records that were added to the table during the previous day, creates HTML reports, and pushes the reports into third-party storage. The item size varies from 1 KB to 4 KB, and the index structure is defined with the date. The developer needs to minimize the read capacity that the application requires from the DynamoDB table. Which DynamoDB API operation should the developer use in the code to meet these requirements?
options: Query
Scan
BatchGetItem
GetItem
questions.explanation: The Query operation lets the application retrieve exactly the items matching the previous day's date range using the table's defined index structure, reading only matching items rather than the whole table, which minimizes the read capacity consumed compared to the alternatives. Scan (B) reads every item in the table regardless of the date filter, consuming far more read capacity, BatchGetItem (C) requires already knowing each item's specific primary key rather than a date-range condition, and GetItem (D) retrieves only a single named item at a time, not a range of items by date.

questions.question: A company is launching a feature that uses an HTTP API built with Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. An API Gateway endpoint performs several independent tasks that run in a Lambda function. The independent tasks can take up to 10 minutes in total to finish running. Users report that the endpoint sometimes returns an HTTP 604 status code. The Lambda function invocations are successful. Which solution will stop the endpoint from returning the HTTP 504 status cade?
options: Increase the Lambda function’s timeout value.
Increase the reserved concurrency of the Lambda function.
Increase the memory that is available to the Lambda function.
Refactor the Lambda function to start an AWS Step Functions state machine.
questions.explanation: Refactoring the Lambda function to start an AWS Step Functions state machine offloads the up-to-10-minute workflow to Step Functions, which can run far longer than API Gateway's fixed maximum integration timeout (29 seconds), avoiding the HTTP 504 caused by API Gateway timing out while waiting on a synchronous Lambda response. Increasing the Lambda function's own timeout (A) does not help since API Gateway's own integration timeout is fixed and shorter than the task's actual duration, and increasing reserved concurrency (B) or memory (C) address throughput and compute speed respectively, neither of which resolves an integration that structurally cannot wait long enough for a multi-minute synchronous response.

questions.question: A company has an application that uses an Amazon Cognito user pool for authentication. A developer needs to add a new REST API that will use the user pool to authenticate requests. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST development effort?
options: Create a new API key and a new usage plan. Associate the API key and the REST API with the usage plan.
Create a Cognito authorizer for the correct user pool. Reference the header that contains the Cognito token.
Create an AWS Lambda token authorizer. Reference the authorization token in the event payload. Authenticate requests based on the token value.
Create an AWS Lambda request authorizer. Reference the authorization header in the event payload. Authenticate requests by using the header value in a request to the Cognito API.
questions.explanation: API Gateway has a native Cognito authorizer type that plugs directly into an existing user pool by referencing the header carrying the token, requiring no custom authorization code. API keys and usage plans (A) authenticate a client application rather than individual pool users, and both Lambda authorizer options (C, D) require writing and maintaining custom authorization logic that duplicates what the built-in Cognito authorizer already does.

questions.question: A developer is testing an AWS Lambda function that has an event source of an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The developer notices that some of the messages the Lambda function processes re-appear in the queue while the messages are being processed. The developer must correct this behavior. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Increase the timeout of the Lambda function.
Increase the visibility timeout of the SQS queue.
Increase the memory allocation of the Lambda function.
Increase the batch size in the event source mapping.
questions.explanation: Increasing the SQS queue's visibility timeout so it comfortably exceeds the Lambda function's actual processing time prevents a message from becoming visible to other consumers again while it is still being processed, which is exactly what was causing messages to reappear mid-processing. Increasing the Lambda function's timeout (A) does not by itself change when SQS makes a message visible again, increasing memory (C) speeds up processing but does not fix a visibility timeout that is simply set too short, and increasing the batch size (D) changes how many messages are retrieved per invocation, it does not address the visibility timeout mismatch causing reappearance.

questions.question: A developer created reusable code that several AWS Lambda functions need to use. The developer bundled the code into a zip archive. The developer needs to deploy the code to AWS and update the Lambda functions to use the code. Which solution will meet this requirement in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Upload the zip archive to Amazon S3. Configure an import path on the Lambda functions to point to the zip archive.
Create a new Lambda function that contains and runs the shared code. Update the existing Lambda functions to invoke the new Lambda function synchronously.
Create a Lambda layer that contains the zip archive. Attach the Lambda layer to the Lambda functions.
Create a Lambda container image that includes the shared code. Use the container image as a Lambda base image for all the functions.
questions.explanation: Creating a Lambda layer from the zip archive and attaching that layer to each Lambda function that needs the shared code lets the reusable code be deployed once, as a versioned artifact, and reused across every function with no per-function code duplication or extra invocation hops, the most operationally efficient option. Uploading the archive to S3 and configuring an 'import path' (A) is not a real Lambda mechanism for loading shared code this way, wrapping the shared code in its own Lambda function invoked synchronously by each of the original functions (B) adds unnecessary invocation latency and cost, and building a full container image per function (D) is more operational overhead than simply attaching a lightweight layer to existing .zip-based functions.

questions.question: A team has an Amazon API Gateway REST API that consists of a single resource and a GET method that is backed by an AWS Lambda integration. A developer makes a change to the Lambda function and deploys the function as a new version. The developer needs to set up a process to test the new version of the function before using the new version in production. The tests must not affect the production REST API. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a new resource in the REST API. Add a GET method to the new resource, and add a Lambda integration to the updated version of the Lambda function. Deploy the new version.

Create a new stage for the REST API. Create a stage variable. Assign the stage variable to the Lambda function. Set the API Gateway integrated Lambda function name to the stage variable. Deploy the new version.
Create a new REST API. Add a resource that has a single GET method that is integrated with the updated version of the Lambda function.
Update the Lambda integration of the existing GET method to point to the updated version of the Lambda function. Deploy the new version.
questions.explanation: Creating a new API Gateway stage and a stage variable that references the updated Lambda function (used in the stage's integration configuration) lets the new version be tested through that stage's own distinct URL, entirely separate from the existing production stage and its GET method, with no impact on production traffic and the least operational overhead. Adding a new resource within the same existing stage (A) still deploys the change alongside the production configuration on the same stage, creating a brand-new separate REST API (C) duplicates the whole API unnecessarily, and directly updating the existing GET method's integration to point at the new version (D) would immediately affect production traffic, which is exactly what needs to be avoided.

questions.question: A developer manages encryption keys in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). The developer must ensure that all encryption keys can be deleted immediately when the keys are no longer required. The developer wants a solution that is highly available and does not require manual management for compute infrastructure. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS KMS managed keys. When the keys are no longer required, schedule the keys for immediate deletion.
Use customer managed keys with imported key material. When the keys are no longer required, delete the imported key material.
Use customer managed keys. When the keys are no longer required, delete the key material.
Use customer managed keys and an AWS CloudHSM key store. When the keys are no longer required, schedule the keys for immediate deletion.
questions.explanation: Deleting the imported key material of a customer managed key with imported key material is immediate, requires no waiting period, and involves no compute infrastructure to manage, making it inherently highly available. AWS managed keys (A) cannot be scheduled for deletion by the customer, standard customer managed keys with AWS-generated material (C) require a mandatory 7-30 day waiting period before the key can be deleted, and a CloudHSM-backed custom key store (D) requires provisioning and managing HSM cluster infrastructure.

questions.question: A company has an ecommerce application. The application's API sends order data to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SOS) queue. A developer needs to modify the application to enrich the order data before the application sends the order data to a fulfillment system. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST development effort?
options: Create an AWS Lambda function to poll the SOS queue. enrich the message data, and send the enriched data to the fulfilment system, Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe the Lambda function to the SNS topic.

Create an AWS Step Functions state machine. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to run the state machine when an order is published to the SQS queue. Map the orders to an AWS Lambda function. Program the Lambda function to perform the data enrichment and to invoke the state machine. Configure the last step of the state machine to send the enriched data to the fulfilment system,

Create an Amazon EMR cluster to read messages from the SQS queue. Configure an EMR job to enrich the order data. Create and configure an Amazon S3 bucket as the output location. Adjust the order fulfilment system to retrieve the enriched files from the S3 bucket.
Create an Amazon EventBridge pipe that uses event enrichment. Configure the SQS queue as a source for the pipe. Set the fulfillment system as the target of the pipe.
questions.explanation: An Amazon EventBridge Pipes pipe configured with event enrichment lets the pipe call an enrichment target (such as a Lambda function or an API) to add data to each message before delivering it onward to the target fulfillment system, all with a single managed, no-code pipe configuration and the least development effort. Building a Lambda function polling the queue plus a separate SNS topic subscription (A) or a Step Functions workflow triggered by an EventBridge rule (B) both require custom orchestration code that a Pipes enrichment step already handles declaratively, and standing up an Amazon EMR cluster (C) is a large-scale batch analytics tool, far heavier than needed for simple per-message enrichment.

questions.question: An application interacts with Amazon Aurora to store and track customer information. The primary database is set up with multiple read replicas for improving the performance of the read queries. However, one of the Aurora replicas is receiving most or all of the traffic, while the other Aurora replica remains idle. How can this issue be resolved?
options: Disable application-level DNS caching.
Enable application-level DNS caching.
Enable application pooling
Disable application pooling
questions.explanation: Aurora read replica DNS endpoints are resolved by clients, and if the application caches that DNS resolution for too long, it can keep sending nearly all read traffic to whichever replica IP it originally resolved and cached, explaining one replica receiving most traffic while another sits idle; disabling application-level DNS caching (or keeping the cache TTL short) lets the client re-resolve and naturally distribute connections across replicas over time. Enabling DNS caching (B) would make the imbalance worse, not better, and application or connection pooling settings (C, D) are not the documented root cause of this specific Aurora reader-endpoint load-imbalance symptom, which is specifically tied to DNS resolution caching behavior.

questions.question: A company runs continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines for its application on AWS CodePipeline. A developer must write unit tests and run them as part of the pipelines before staging the artifacts for testing. How should the developer incorporate unit tests as part of CI/CD pipelines?
options: Create a separate CodePipeline pipeline to run unit tests.
Update the AWS CodeBuild build specification to include a phase for running unit tests.
Install the AWS CodeDeploy agent on an Amazon EC2 instance to run unit tests.
Create a testing branch in a git repository for the pipelines to run unit tests.
questions.explanation: Updating the CodeBuild build specification (buildspec) to add a phase that runs the unit tests integrates testing directly into the existing CodeBuild-based build stage of the pipeline, requiring no new pipeline, branch, or separate compute infrastructure. Creating an entirely separate CodePipeline pipeline just to run unit tests (A) duplicates pipeline infrastructure unnecessarily, installing the CodeDeploy agent on an EC2 instance to run tests (C) misapplies CodeDeploy, which is a deployment tool rather than a test runner, and creating a separate testing branch (D) does not itself cause CI/CD pipeline stages to run unit tests, that requires an actual build/test configuration change like updating the buildspec.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting a three-tier application, which is deployed on Amazon EC2 instances. There is a connectivity problem between the application servers and the database servers. Which AWS services or tools should be used to identity the faulty component? (Choose two.)
options: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon VPC Flow Logs
Network access control lists
AWS Config rules
questions.explanation: VPC Flow Logs show which traffic is accepted or rejected between tiers, and NACLs provide the stateless subnet-level allow and deny rules to inspect, so together they isolate the faulty network component. CloudTrail records API calls rather than packet flow; Trusted Advisor gives guidance rather than packet evidence; Config rules evaluate configuration compliance rather than live connectivity.

questions.question: A company runs a new application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The company needs to deploy updates to the application. The updates must not cause any downtime for application users. The deployment must forward a specified percentage of incoming client traffic to a new application version during an evaluation period. Which deployment type will meet these requirements?
options: rolling
traffic-splitting
in-place
immutable
questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk's traffic-splitting deployment policy deploys the new version to a separate set of instances and then forwards a specified percentage of incoming client traffic to those new instances during an evaluation period, before shifting the rest, directly matching the requirement to forward a specified percentage of traffic to the new version with zero downtime. Rolling (A) updates the existing instances in sequential batches rather than splitting live traffic by percentage to a separate new set of instances, in-place (C) updates instances directly with potential brief disruption, and immutable (D) shifts all traffic to new instances only after they pass health checks, rather than gradually forwarding a specified percentage during an evaluation window.

questions.question: A developer is making changes to a custom application that uses AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Which solutions will update the Elastic Beanstalk environment with the new application version after the developer completes the changes? (Choose two.)
options: Package the application code into a zip file. Use the AWS Management Console to upload the .zip file and deploy the packaged application.
Package the application code into a .tar file. Use the AWS Management Console to create a new application version from the .tar file. Update the environment by using the AWS CLI.
Package the application code into a .tar file. Use the AWS Management Console to upload the .tar file and deploy the packaged application.
Package the application code into a .zip file. Use the AWS CL to create a new application version from the .zip file and to update the environment.
Package the application code into a .zip file. Use the AWS Management Console to create a new application version from the .zip file. Rebuild the environment by using the AWS CLI.
questions.explanation: Packaging the application into a .zip file and either uploading and deploying it directly through the Management Console, or creating a new application version from the .zip file and updating the environment through the AWS CLI, are both standard, fully supported Elastic Beanstalk workflows for deploying a new application version using the .zip format Elastic Beanstalk expects. Options describing a .tar file (B, C) do not match Elastic Beanstalk's supported source bundle format for this workflow, and 'rebuilding the environment' via the CLI after creating a version from the console (E) is a more disruptive action (a full environment rebuild) than the straightforward version update the requirement calls for.

questions.question: A developer needs to write an AWS CloudFormation template on a local machine and deploy a CloudFormation stack to AWS. What must the developer do to complete these tasks?
options: Install the AWS CLI. Configure the AWS CLI by using an IAM user name and password.
Install the AWS CLI. Configure the AWS CLI by using an SSH key.
Install the AWS CLI, Configure the AWS CLI by using an IAM user access key and secret key.
Install an AWS software development kit (SDK). Configure the SDK by using an X.509 certificate.
questions.explanation: Deploying CloudFormation stacks from a local machine through the CLI requires configuring the CLI with credentials it understands, an IAM access key ID and secret access key, the standard mechanism for programmatic access. A username and password (A) is a console-login credential type the CLI's provider chain does not accept, an SSH key (B) is used for things like EC2 login or Git rather than AWS API authentication, and an X.509 certificate (D) is a legacy credential type not used for standard SDK or CLI configuration.

questions.question: A large company has its application components distributed across multiple AWS accounts. The company needs to collect and visualize trace data across these accounts. What should be used to meet these requirements?
options: AWS X-Ray
Amazon CloudWatch
Amazon VPC flow logs
Amazon OpenSearch Service
questions.explanation: X-Ray supports cross-account tracing so trace segments from components in different accounts can be collected and visualized together. CloudWatch is account-scoped for this use case; VPC flow logs capture packets rather than request traces; OpenSearch would require building a custom trace pipeline.

questions.question: A developer must cache dependent artifacts from Maven Central, a public package repository, as part of an application’s build pipeline. The build pipeline has an AWS CodeArtifact repository where artifacts of the build are published. The developer needs a solution that requires minimum changes to the build pipeline. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Modify the existing CodeAriifact repository to associate an upstream repository with the public package repository.
Create a new CodeAtfact repository that has an external connection to the public package repository.
Create a new CodeAifact domain that contains a new repository that has an external connection to the public package repository.
Modify the CodeAnifact repository resource policy to allow artifacts to be fetched from the public package repository.
questions.explanation: Modifying the existing CodeArtifact repository to associate an upstream repository configured with a connection to the public Maven Central repository lets CodeArtifact itself fetch, cache, and serve public dependencies through the existing repository with no changes to how the build pipeline already references it, the least change to the pipeline. Creating an entirely new repository or domain (B, C) requires updating the build pipeline to point at the new repository, and modifying the repository's resource policy (D) controls access permissions, it does not establish the actual upstream connection needed to fetch and cache public packages.

questions.question: A developer is creating an AWS Step Functions state machine to handle an order processing workflow. When the state machine receives an order, the state machine pauses until the order has been confirmed. A record that is added to an Amazon DynamoDB table by another service confirms each order. The developer must complete the order processing workflow. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Update the state machine to query the DynamoDB table by using the DynamoDB GetItem state to determine whether a record exists. If the record does exist, continue to the next state. If the record does not exist, wait 5 minutes and check again.

Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to a DynamoDB table stream. Configure the Lambda function to run when a new record is added to the table. When the Lambda function receives the appropriate record, run the redrive execution command on the running state machine.

Subscribe an AWS Lambda function to the DynamoDB table stream. Configure the Lambda function to run when a new record is added to the table. When the Lambda function receives the appropriate record, stop the current state machine invocation and start a new invocation.

Invoke an AWS Lambda function from the state machine. Configure the Lambda function to continuously poll the DynamoDB table for the appropriate record and to return when a record exists. Continue the state machine invocation when the Lambda function returns. If the Lambda function times out, then fail the state machine.
questions.explanation: Since another service inserts a confirming record into DynamoDB, subscribing a Lambda function to that table's DynamoDB stream lets the function react the instant the confirmation record appears, and calling the state machine's redrive execution capability resumes the paused state machine to continue processing the now-confirmed order, which is the documented mechanism for resuming a Standard Step Functions execution rather than starting a duplicate one. Polling for the record inside the state machine using repeated GetItem calls and a wait loop (A) works but polls inefficiently rather than reacting immediately to the stream event, and stopping the current execution and starting an entirely new one (C) loses the original execution's state and history rather than properly resuming it, while continuously polling from inside a long-running Lambda function until a record appears (D) is a wasteful, non-event-driven approach compared to reacting to the stream directly.

questions.question: A developer is writing a web application that must share secure documents with end users. The documents are stored in a private Amazon S3 bucket. The application must allow only authenticated users to download specific documents when requested, and only for a duration of 15 minutes. How can the developer meet these requirements?
options: Copy the documents to a separate S3 bucket that has a lifecycle policy for deletion after 15 minutes.
Create a presigned S3 URL using the AWS SDK with an expiration time of 15 minutes.
Use server-side encryption with AWS KMS managed keys (SSE-KMS) and download the documents using HTTPS.
Modify the S3 bucket policy to only allow specific users to download the documents. Revert the change after 15 minutes.
questions.explanation: A presigned URL generated with an explicit 15-minute expiration is the S3 mechanism for granting time-limited, per-request download access to a specific private object, with no bucket policy or object changes needed. Copying to a bucket with a lifecycle deletion policy (A) is operationally fragile and destroys the original, SSE-KMS plus HTTPS (C) addresses encryption rather than time-limited authorization, and manually toggling and reverting a bucket policy (D) is heavy and error-prone compared with a self-expiring signed link.

questions.question: A company is developing a set of AWS Lambda functions to process data. The Lambda functions need to use a common third-party library as a dependency. The library is frequently updated with new features and bug fixes. The company wants to ensure that the Lambda functions always use the latest version of the library. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Store the dependency and the function code in an Amazon S3 bucket.
Create a Lambda layer that includes the library. Attach the layer to each Lambda function.
Install the dependency in an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Attach the file system to each Lambda function.
Create a new Lambda function to load the library. Configure the existing Lambda functions to invoke the new Lambda function when the existing functions need to use the library.
questions.explanation: A Lambda layer containing the shared third-party library, attached to each function, lets all the functions reference the exact same versioned library artifact, and publishing a new layer version to pick up library updates (and pointing functions at the new version) is a purpose-built, low-overhead mechanism for exactly this kind of shared, updatable dependency across multiple functions. Storing the dependency in S3 alongside the function code (A) or in an EFS file system attached to every function (C) both require custom code to load the library at runtime rather than using Lambda's native layer attachment, and creating a separate Lambda function just to load the library for other functions to invoke (D) adds unnecessary invocation overhead and complexity compared to a shared layer.

questions.question: A company’s application includes an Amazon DynamoDB table for product orders. The table has a primary partition key of orderId and has no sort key. The company is adding a new feature that requires the application to query the table by using the customerId attribute. Which solution will provide this query functionality?
options: Change the existing primary key by setting customerId as the sort key.
Create a new global secondary index (GSI) on the table with a partition key of customerId.
Create a new local secondary index (LSI) on the table with a partition key of customerId.
Create a new local secondary index (LSI) on the table with a partition key of orderId and a sort key of customerId.
questions.explanation: Creating a new GSI with customerId as its partition key lets the application query orders directly by customer, something the base table's orderId-only key does not support, without disrupting the table's existing primary key or access patterns. Changing the existing primary key to add customerId as a sort key (A) would break existing lookups by orderId alone, and both LSI options (C, D) must share the base table's existing partition key (orderId), so neither can use customerId as an LSI's own partition key.

questions.question: A company hosts applications on premises. The on-premises servers generate audit logs that are available through an HTTP endpoint. The company needs an automated solution to regularly ingest and store large volumes of audit data from the on-premises servers. The company also needs to perform queries on the audit data. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Export the audit logs. Upload the logs to Amazon S3. Import the logs to an Amazon RDS DB instance.

Create an AWS Lambda function to call the HTTP endpoint to fetch audit logs. Configure an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to invoke the Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to push the logs to AWS CloudTrail Lake.
Use AWS DataSync to transfer audit logs to an Amazon S3 bucket. Load the logs into an Amazon S3 bucket. Use Amazon Athena to query the bucket.
Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the on-premises servers. Give the agent the ability to push audit logs to CloudWatch. Use CloudWatch Insights to query the logs.
questions.explanation: Installing the CloudWatch agent on the on-premises servers to push logs directly into CloudWatch Logs, then using CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the ingested audit data, is a managed, purpose-built AWS mechanism for exactly this kind of log ingestion and querying, requiring the least amount of custom orchestration. Manually exporting and periodically uploading logs to S3 and importing into RDS (A) is a manual, batch-oriented process rather than an automated regular ingestion pipeline, a scheduled Lambda function polling an HTTP endpoint (B) requires the on-premises servers to expose logs via HTTP, which is not stated as available in a way suited for bulk ingestion, and AWS DataSync (C) is designed for transferring files/data between storage systems, not for querying structured log content the way CloudWatch Logs Insights does.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that includes an AWS Lambda function that is written in .NET Core. The Lambda function’s code needs to interact with Amazon DynamoDB tables and Amazon S3 buckets. The developer must minimize the Lambda function’s deployment time and invocation duration. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Increase the Lambda function’s memory.
Include the entire AWS SDK for .NET in the Lambda function’s deployment package.
Include only the AWS SDK for .NET modules for DynamoDB and Amazon S3 in the Lambda function’s deployment package.
Configure the Lambda function to download the AWS SDK for .NET from an S3 bucket at runtime.
questions.explanation: Including only the specific AWS SDK for .NET modules needed for DynamoDB and Amazon S3, rather than the entire SDK, reduces both the deployment package's size (speeding up deployment) and the amount of code that needs to be loaded and JIT-compiled at cold start (speeding up invocation), directly addressing both stated requirements. Increasing memory (A) can help invocation speed somewhat but does not address the deployment package size or the root inefficiency of bundling unnecessary SDK modules, bundling the entire SDK (B) works against both requirements, and downloading the SDK from S3 at runtime (D) adds unpredictable latency and complexity on every cold start rather than reducing it.

questions.question: A development team has an Amazon API Gateway REST API that is backed by an AWS Lambda function. Users have reported performance issues for the Lambda function. The development team identified the source of the issues as a cold start of the Lambda function. The development team needs to reduce the time needed for the Lambda function to initialize. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Change the Lambda concurrency to reserved concurrency.
Increase the timeout of the Lambda function.
Increase the memory allocation of the Lambda function.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Provisioned concurrency keeps the chosen number of Lambda execution environments initialized so cold starts are avoided and initialization time drops. Reserved concurrency only caps throughput; timeout and memory settings do not pre-warm environments.

questions.question: A video streaming company has a pipe in Amazon EventBridge Pipes that uses an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue as an event source. The pipe publishes all source events to a target EventBridge event bus. Before events are published, the pipe uses an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the stream status of each event from a database and adds the stream status to each source event. The company wants the pipe to publish events to the event bus only if the video stream has a status of ready. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Add a filter step to the pipe that will match on a stream status of ready.
Update the Lambda function to return only video streams that have a status of ready.
Include a filter for a status of ready in all EventBridge rules that subscribe to the event bus.
Add an input transformer to the pipe output that filters streams that have a status of ready.
questions.explanation: In EventBridge Pipes, the Filter step runs before the enrichment step in the pipeline, so a dedicated filter on the pipe cannot see the stream-status field the enrichment Lambda function itself adds; instead, updating the enrichment Lambda function to return an empty response for any event whose stream is not ready causes Pipes to drop that event and never publish it to the target event bus, which is the documented way to use an enrichment step itself as a post-enrichment filter. Adding a Filter step to the pipe (A) would run before enrichment and so cannot filter on the enriched stream-status value, filtering inside EventBridge rules that subscribe to the event bus (C) would still publish every event to the bus regardless of readiness, and an input transformer on the pipe's output (D) reshapes the event payload, it does not drop non-matching events.

questions.question: A developer needs to build a workflow to handle messages that are sent to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. When a message reaches the queue, the workflow must implement a delay before invoking an AWS Lambda function to process the message. Which solution will meet this requirement in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Create an AWS Step Functions state machine to process the SQS queue. Use a Wait state to delay the Lambda function’s processing for the required number of seconds after message delivery to the SQS queue. Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke the state machine every 5 minutes.

Configure the Lambda function to poll the SQS queue. Update the Lambda code to republish each message with a custom attribute that contains a future time when the message should be fully processed. Update the Lambda code to fully process messages when the custom attribute’s future time has passed.

Set the DelaySeconds value of the SQS queue to be the number of seconds required to delay delivery of the messages. Add an event source mapping for the Lambda function. Specify the SQS queue as a source.

Set the Visibility Timeout value of the SQS queue to be the number of seconds required to delay delivery of the messages. Add an event source mapping for the Lambda function. Specify the SQS queue as a source.
questions.explanation: Setting the SQS queue's DelaySeconds to the required delay postpones a message's initial visibility to consumers by that many seconds after it is sent, and adding an event source mapping between the queue and the Lambda function lets Lambda automatically poll and invoke on the delayed messages once they become visible, all using native SQS/Lambda integration features with no custom code. A Step Functions state machine with a Wait state invoked every 5 minutes by EventBridge (A) adds unnecessary orchestration and imprecise timing compared to SQS's native per-message delay, republishing messages with a custom future-time attribute (B) reimplements delayed delivery that SQS already provides natively, and increasing the visibility timeout (D) affects how long an in-flight message stays hidden from other consumers during processing, it does not delay a message's very first delivery the way DelaySeconds does.

questions.question: A company is building an application to accept data from customers. The data must be encrypted at rest and in transit. The application uses an Amazon API Gateway API that resolves to AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda functions store the data in an Amazon Aurora MySQL DB cluster. The application worked properly during testing. A developer configured an Amazon CloudFront distribution with field-level encryption that uses an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key. After the configuration of the distribution, the application behaved unexpectedly. All the data in the database changed from plaintext to ciphertext. The developer must ensure that the data is not stored in the database as the ciphertext from the CloudFront field-level encryption. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Change the CloudFront Viewer protocol policy from “HTTP and HTTPS” to “HTTPS only.”
Add a Lambda function that uses the KMS key to decrypt the data fields before saving the data to the database.
Enable encryption on the DB cluster by using the same KMS key that is used in CloudFront.
Request and deploy a new SSL certificate to use with the CloudFront distribution.
questions.explanation: Since CloudFront's field-level encryption already encrypted the sensitive fields with the specified KMS key by the time the request reaches the Lambda functions, those functions need to explicitly decrypt the fields using the same key before writing plaintext to Aurora, because field-level encryption is meant to protect data in transit through the CDN and API layer, not to become the database's storage format. Changing the CloudFront viewer protocol policy (A) or issuing a new SSL certificate (D) address transport-level HTTPS settings unrelated to the payload transformation, and enabling encryption on the DB cluster (C) encrypts storage at rest but does not reverse the field-level ciphertext already present in the incoming payload.

questions.question: A company offers a business-to-business software service that runs on dedicated infrastructure deployed in each customer’s AWS account. Before a feature release, the company needs to run integration tests on real AWS test infrastructure. The test infrastructure consists of Amazon EC2 instances and an Amazon RDS database. A developer must set up a continuous delivery process that will provision the test infrastructure across the different AWS accounts. The developer then must run the integration tests. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative effort?
options: Use AWS CodeDeploy with AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy the infrastructure. Use Amazon CodeGuru to run the tests.
Use AWS CodePipeline with AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy the infrastructure. Use AWS CodeBuild to run the tests.
Use AWS CodePipeline with AWS CloudFormation change sets to deploy the infrastructure. Use a CloudFormation custom resource to run the tests.
Use AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) templates with AWS CloudFormation change sets to deploy the infrastructure. Use AWS CodeDeploy to run the tests.
questions.explanation: AWS CodePipeline paired with CloudFormation StackSets deploys the same test infrastructure template consistently across the different customer AWS accounts with minimal per-account setup, and AWS CodeBuild is a natural, flexible place to run the actual integration test suite as a pipeline stage. AWS CodeDeploy (A) is designed for deploying application code to existing compute rather than provisioning brand-new cross-account infrastructure, and Amazon CodeGuru (A) analyzes code quality/performance rather than running custom integration test suites, CloudFormation change sets (C) preview updates to a single stack rather than provisioning consistently across many separate accounts the way StackSets does, and running tests via a CloudFormation custom resource (C) or through CodeDeploy (D) both misapply tools not meant for orchestrating and running a general integration test suite the way CodeBuild is.

questions.question: A developer is creating an application that uses an AWS Lambda function to transform and load data from an Amazon S3 bucket. When the developer tests the application, the developer finds that some invocations of the Lambda function are slower than others. The developer needs to update the Lambda function to have predictable invocation durations that run with low latency. Any initialization activities, such as loading libraries and instantiating clients, must run during allocation time rather than during actual function invocations. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Choose two.)
options: Create a schedule group in Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke the Lambda function.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function to have the necessary number of execution environments.
Use the $LATEST version of the Lambda function.
Configure reserved concurrency for the Lambda function to have the necessary number of execution environments.
Deploy changes, and publish a new version of the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Publishing a version of the Lambda function and configuring provisioned concurrency for it pre-initializes the specified number of execution environments in advance, running all initialization code (such as loading libraries and instantiating clients) ahead of time so that actual invocations experience predictable, low latency rather than paying initialization cost during the invocation itself. Using an EventBridge schedule group to invoke the function (A) does not itself address cold-start unpredictability, using the $LATEST unpublished version (C) is explicitly not supported for provisioned concurrency (which requires a published version or alias), and reserved concurrency (D) only caps how many concurrent invocations are allowed, it does not pre-initialize execution environments the way provisioned concurrency does.

questions.question: A developer created an AWS Lambda function named ProcessMessages. The Lambda function is invoked asynchronously when a message is published to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic named InputTopic. The developer uses a second SNS topic named ErrorTopic to handle alerts of failures for other services. The developer wants to receive notifications from the ErrorTopic SNS topic when the ProcessMessages Lambda function fails to process a message. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Configure a subscription for the ErrorTopic SNS topic. Configure a filter policy for failures. Specify the ProcessMessages Lambda function as the endpoint.
Configure a failure destination for the ProcessMessages Lambda function. Specify the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the ErrorTopic SNS topic as the destination ARN.
Configure a trigger for the ProcessMessages Lambda function. Specify the ErrorTopic SNS topic as the trigger topic. Configure a filter policy on the topic for failures
Configure a delivery policy on the ErrorTopic SNS topic. Configure a filter policy for failures. Specify the Lambda function as the input endpoint.
questions.explanation: Configuring a failure destination for the ProcessMessages Lambda function's asynchronous invocation, pointed at the ErrorTopic SNS topic's ARN, is Lambda's native, built-in mechanism to automatically publish invocation failure details to a separate destination with no additional code. Subscribing the ErrorTopic to notify the ProcessMessages function itself with a filter policy (A) has the direction backwards, since ErrorTopic is meant to receive failure notifications, not send them to the function that is failing, adding a 'trigger' from ErrorTopic to the function (C) similarly misapplies the relationship, and a 'delivery policy' with a filter for failures on ErrorTopic (D) is not how Lambda invocation failures are captured and routed to a separate topic.

questions.question: A company is developing a new application that uses Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, and AWS Lambda resources. The company wants to allow employees to access the AWS Management Console by using existing credentials that the company stores and manages in an on-premises Microsoft Active Directory. Each employee must have a specific level of access to the AWS resources that is based on the employee’s role. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure AWS Directory Service to create an Active Directory in AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. Establish a trust relationship with the on-premises Active Directory. Configure IAM roles and trust policies to give the employees access to the AWS resources.
Use LDAP to directly integrate the on-premises Active Directory with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Map Active Directory groups to IAM roles to control access to AWS resources.

Implement a custom identity broker to authenticate users into the on-premises Active Directory. Configure the identity broker to use AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) to grant authorized users IAM role based access to the AWS resources.
Configure Amazon Cognito to federate users into the on-premises Active Directory. Use Cognito user pools to manage user identities and to manage user access to the AWS resources.
questions.explanation: AWS Directory Service can create a managed Active Directory that establishes a trust relationship with the existing on-premises AD, letting employees federate into the AWS Management Console with their existing credentials, and mapping Active Directory groups to IAM roles then controls role-based access, all without a custom identity broker. Direct LDAP integration with IAM (B) is not a supported federation mechanism, a custom identity broker with STS (C) duplicates functionality AWS Directory Service already provides, and Cognito (D) federates users into Cognito pools for application access rather than into the AWS Management Console.

questions.question: A company has an Amazon DynamoDB table that contains records of users that have signed up for a trial of the company’s product. The company is using a spreadsheet to track data about the product trial. The company needs to ensure the spreadsheet is automatically updated with the latest information when individual trials begin, are updated, or finish. Which solution will meet these requirements?
