options: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster from the table. Set the view type to old image. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the cluster data to update the spreadsheet. Subscribe the Lambda function to the cluster.

Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster from the table. Set the view type to new image. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the cluster data to update the spreadsheet. Subscribe the Lambda function to the cluster.
Enable a DynamoDB stream for the table. Set the view type to new image. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the stream data to update the spreadsheet. Subscribe the Lambda function to the stream.
Enable a DynamoDB stream for the table. Set the view type to old image. Create an AWS Lambda function that uses the stream data to update the spreadsheet. Subscribe the Lambda function to the stream.
questions.explanation: Enabling a DynamoDB stream on the table with the view type set to new image, then subscribing a Lambda function to the stream that uses the new item data to update the spreadsheet, captures every insert and update to trial records in near real time and reflects the current state of each trial, exactly matching the requirement. Using DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as if it were a change-capture mechanism (A, B) misapplies DAX, which is a read-caching layer rather than a stream of table changes, and setting the stream view type to old image (D) would only expose the pre-change data rather than the new, updated values needed to keep the spreadsheet current.

questions.question: A developer is launching a global application that delivers content to multiple countries. The developer needs to serve specific content based on the country of each user and each user’s primary language. The developer must ensure that content is served reliably and with low latency. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator to resolve requests to the API. Configure endpoint groups on the accelerator. Attach listeners for each country and language.

Store the content in a centralized Amazon S3 bucket. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket. Create an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone that includes the endpoint for the S3 bucket. Create records in Route 53 that use geoproximity and geolocation routing policies.

Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API. Connect the REST API to AWS WAF. Use geo match statements and regex match statements to allow or deny requests based on the labels returned from web request evaluations.

Configure an Amazon CloudFront distribution that uses the application as an origin. Configure the distribution to forward the Accept-Language header and the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header to the origin.
questions.explanation: Configuring a CloudFront distribution to forward the Accept-Language header (the user's browser language preference) and the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header (CloudFront's own geolocation of the request) to the origin lets the application serve country- and language-specific content while benefiting from CloudFront's globally distributed, low-latency, highly available edge network. AWS Global Accelerator with per-country listeners (A) is designed for improving network path performance to fixed endpoints rather than for content localization by header, S3 Transfer Acceleration with Route 53 geoproximity/geolocation routing (B) optimizes upload/transfer speed and DNS-level routing rather than per-request header-based content selection, and using AWS WAF geo match rules to allow or deny requests (C) controls access, it does not serve different content based on language and country the way header forwarding does.

questions.question: A company generates SSL certificates from a third-party provider. The company imports the certificates into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to use with public web applications. A developer must implement a solution to notify the company’s security team 90 days before an imported certificate expires. The company already has configured an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The company also has configured an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that has the security team’s email address as a subscriber. Which solution will provide the security team with the required notification about certificates?
options: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that specifies the ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event type. Set the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule’s target.

Create an AWS Lambda function to search for all certificates that are expiring within 90 days. Program the Lambda function to send each identified certificate’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in a message to the SQS queue.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that is invoked by each certificate’s expiration notification from AWS CloudTrail. Create an AWS Lambda function to send each certificate's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in a message to the SQS queue.

Configure AWS Config with the acm-certificate-expiration-check managed rule to run every 24 hours. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that includes an event pattern that specifies the Config Rules Compliance Change detail type and the configured rule. Set the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule’s target.
questions.explanation: An EventBridge rule that matches the ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event type, with the existing SNS topic (which already has the security team subscribed by email) as its target, uses ACM's own native expiration event and requires no custom code to detect expiring certificates or determine the 90-day threshold, since ACM's managed monitoring already emits this event automatically. Building a custom Lambda function to search for expiring certificates (B) reimplements detection logic ACM already provides as a native event, and routing through a Step Functions workflow invoked from CloudTrail (C) is a heavier, more custom mechanism than simply targeting the existing SNS topic directly from the native ACM EventBridge event.

questions.question: A developer is working on a new authorization mechanism for an application. The developer must create an Amazon API Gateway API and must test JSON Web Token (JWT) authorization on the API. The developer must use the built-in authorizer and must avoid managing the code with custom logic. The developer needs to define an API route that is available at /auth to test the authorizer configuration. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a WebSocket API and the /auth route. Configure and attach the JWT authorizer to the API. Deploy the API.
Create a WebSocket API and the /auth route. Create and configure an AWS Lambda authorizer. Attach the Lambda authorizer to the API. Deploy the API.
Create an HTTP API and the /auth route. Create and configure an AWS Lambda authorizer. Attach the Lambda authorizer to the /auth route. Deploy the API.
Create an HTTP API and the /auth route. Configure the JWT authorizer. Attach the JWT authorizer to the /auth route. Deploy the API.
questions.explanation: API Gateway HTTP APIs support a native JWT authorizer type that validates standard JSON Web Tokens with zero custom code, exactly matching the requirement to test JWT authorization while avoiding custom logic. WebSocket APIs (A, B) are for persistent bidirectional connections, unrelated to a simple JWT-protected route, and a Lambda authorizer on an HTTP API (C) would require writing custom authorization logic, which the requirement explicitly wants to avoid.

questions.question: A company is creating a new application that gives users the ability to upload and share short video files. The average size of the video files is 10 MB. After a user uploads a file, a message needs to be placed into an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue so the file can be processed. The files need to be accessible for processing within 5 minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
options: Write the files to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Add the S3 location of the files to the SQS queue.
Write the files to Amazon S3 Standard. Add the S3 location of the files to the SQS queue.
Write the files to an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) General Purpose SSD volume. Add the EBS location of the files to the SQS queue.
Write messages that contain the contents of the uploaded files to the SQS queue.
questions.explanation: Writing the uploaded video files to S3 Standard, which provides millisecond-level access well within the 5-minute processing requirement, and simply passing the S3 object location (not the file content itself) in the SQS message, keeps message sizes small (SQS has a 256 KB message size limit) and cost low. S3 Glacier Deep Archive (A) has retrieval times measured in hours, far exceeding the 5-minute requirement, an EBS volume (C) is attached to a single EC2 instance rather than being a scalable shared object store suited to this workload, and embedding entire file contents directly in SQS messages (D) would not fit within SQS's 256 KB message size limit for typical 10 MB video files.

questions.question: A developer is updating the code for an AWS Lambda function to add new capabilities. The Lambda function has version aliases for production and development environments that run separate versions of the function. The developer needs to configure a staging environment for the Lambda function to handle invocations to both the development version and the production version. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create a weighted alias that references the production version of the function and the updated version of the function.
Add a Network Load Balancer. Add the production version of the function and updated version of the function as targets.
Use AWS CodeDeploy to create a linear traffic shifting deployment
Create a tag for the Lambda function that contains the production version and updated version of the code.
questions.explanation: Creating a weighted alias that references both the production version and the updated version, with the desired weight split between them, lets a single alias serve invocations from both the development and production traffic paths simultaneously in whatever proportion is configured, using Lambda's native traffic-splitting alias mechanism with no extra infrastructure. Adding a Network Load Balancer with the two versions as separate targets (B) is not how Lambda functions are typically load balanced (they don't register as NLB targets this way for version splitting), CodeDeploy's linear traffic shifting (C) is meant for a one-directional gradual rollout to full production rather than a stable, ongoing staging split between two versions, and a resource tag (D) is metadata, it has no mechanism for routing invocations between two code versions.

questions.question: A developer has implemented an AWS Lambda function that inserts new customers into an Amazon RDS database. The function is expected to run hundreds of times each hour. The function and RDS database are in the same VPC. The function is configured to use 512 MB of RAM and is based on the following pseudo code: After successfully testing the function multiple times, the developer notices that the execution time is longer than expected. What should the developer do to improve performance?
options: Increase the reserved concurrency of the Lambda function.
Increase the size of the RDS database to facilitate an increased number of database connections each hour.
Move the database connection and close statement out of the handler. Place the connection in the global space.
Replace Amazon RDS with Amazon DynamoDB to implement control over the number of writes per second.
questions.explanation: Moving the database connection setup (and its close statement) outside the Lambda handler and into the function's global scope lets the connection be established once per execution environment and then reused across warm invocations, avoiding the overhead of establishing a new database connection on every single invocation, which is the standard Lambda performance best practice for this exact symptom. Increasing reserved concurrency (A) does not reduce per-invocation latency, it only controls how many invocations run in parallel, resizing the RDS database (B) addresses connection capacity rather than the per-invocation connection-setup overhead actually causing the slowdown, and replacing RDS with DynamoDB (D) is a much larger architectural change than simply fixing where the connection is established in the code.

questions.question: A developer is troubleshooting the permissions of an application that needs to make changes to an Amazon RDS database. The developer has access to the IAM role that the application is using. Which command structure should the developer use to test the role permissions?
options: aws sts assume-role
aws iam attach-role-policy
aws ssm resume-session
aws rds add-role-to-db-cluster
questions.explanation: To directly test what a specific IAM role's permissions actually allow, the developer assumes that role with sts assume-role and then makes calls using the resulting temporary credentials, exercising exactly the permission set the application uses. attach-role-policy (B) modifies the role instead of testing it, ssm resume-session (C) opens a Session Manager shell unrelated to testing IAM permissions, and RDS's add-role-to-db-cluster command (D) associates an IAM role with a cluster for feature access, it does not test a role's permissions.

questions.question: A gaming company has deployed a web portal on AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The company sometimes needs to deploy new versions three or four times in a day. The company needs to deploy new features for all users as quickly as possible. The solution must minimize performance impact and must maximize availability. What solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use a rolling deployment policy to deploy to Amazon EC2 instances.
Use an immutable deployment policy to deploy to Amazon EC2 instances.
Use an all-at-once deployment policy to deploy to Amazon EC2 instances.
Use a-canary deployment strategy to deploy changes to Amazon EC2 instances.
questions.explanation: An immutable deployment policy provisions an entirely new, separate set of EC2 instances for the new version and only shifts traffic to them once they pass health checks, so the existing fleet keeps serving all requests at full performance and availability throughout the deployment, with automatic rollback (simply terminating the new instances) if health checks fail, ideal for frequent daily deployments. A rolling deployment (A) reduces available capacity on the existing fleet during each batch update, all-at-once (C) causes a period of unavailability while every instance updates simultaneously, and canary deployment (D) is not an Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy type at all for EC2-based environments.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function generates a 3 MB JSON file and then uploads it to an Amazon S3 bucket daily. The file contains sensitive information, so the developer must ensure that it is encrypted before uploading to the bucket. Which of the following modifications should the developer make to ensure that the data is encrypted before uploading it to the bucket?
options: Use the default AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key for Amazon S3 in the Lambda function code.
Use the S3 managed key and call the GenerateDataKey API to encrypt the file.
Use the GenerateDataKey API, then use that data key to encrypt the file in the Lambda function code.
Use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key for Amazon S3 in the Lambda function code.
questions.explanation: For a 3 MB file, too large for KMS's Encrypt API single-call size limit of about 4 KB, the correct client-side envelope encryption pattern is calling GenerateDataKey to get a data key, then using that data key locally to symmetrically encrypt the file before uploading. Referencing 'the default S3 KMS key' or 'the S3 managed key' without an actual data-key step (A, B) conflates SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS with client-side encryption, and using a customer managed key directly in code without the data-key step (D) does not describe how KMS handles bulk file encryption.

questions.question: A company is building a social media application. A developer is modifying an AWS Lambda function that updates a database with data that tracks each user's online activity. A web application server uses the AWS SDK to invoke the Lambda function. The developer has tested the new Lambda code and is ready to deploy the code into production. However, the developer wants to allow only a small percentage of the invocations from the AWS SDK to call the new code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure a Lambda version that has a specific weight value for the updated Lambda function.
Create an alias for the Lambda function. Configure a specific weight value for the updated version.
Create an Application Load Balancer. Specify weighted target groups for the original Lambda function and the updated Lambda function.
Create a Network Load Balancer. Specify weighted target groups for the original Lambda function and the updated Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Creating an alias for the Lambda function and configuring a specific weight value on it for the updated version implements Lambda's native weighted-alias traffic-shifting feature, letting only a small, precisely controlled percentage of invocations reach the new code while the rest continue on the stable version, with no additional infrastructure. Lambda function versions themselves do not carry a 'weight value' directly (A); weighting is configured on an alias that points to multiple versions, and introducing an Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer with weighted target groups (C, D) adds unnecessary infrastructure when Lambda aliases already provide this weighted-routing capability natively.

questions.question: An Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream is receiving customer data that contains personally identifiable information. A developer needs to remove pattern-based customer identifiers from the data and store the modified data in an Amazon S3 bucket. What should the developer do to meet these requirements?
options: Implement Firehose data transformation as an AWS Lambda function. Configure the function to remove the customer identifiers. Set an Amazon S3 bucket as the destination of the delivery stream.

Launch an Amazon EC2 instance. Set the EC2 instance as the destination of the delivery stream. Run an application on the EC2 instance to remove the customer identifiers. Store the transformed data in an Amazon S3 bucket.

Create an Amazon OpenSearch Service instance. Set the OpenSearch Service instance as the destination of the delivery stream. Use search and replace to remove the customer identifiers. Export the data to an Amazon S3 bucket.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow to remove the customer identifiers. As the last step in the workflow, store the transformed data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Set the workflow as the destination of the delivery stream.
questions.explanation: Implementing Firehose's built-in data transformation as a Lambda function invoked on each batch of records lets the PII removal happen inline before delivery, with an S3 bucket configured as the destination of the transformed data, using Firehose's native transformation feature exactly as intended. Routing through a self-managed EC2 instance (B) or an OpenSearch Service instance used only for search-and-replace (C) both add unnecessary infrastructure Firehose's built-in Lambda transformation already avoids, and Step Functions (D) is not a supported Firehose delivery destination for this kind of per-record transformation.

questions.question: A developer is building a three-tier web application that should be able to handle a minimum of 5000 requests per minute. Requirements state that the web tier should be completely stateless while the application maintains session state for the users. How can session data be externalized, keeping latency at the LOWEST possible value?
options: Create an Amazon RDS instance, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage a database inside the RDS database instance for session data storage.

Implement a shared file system solution across the underlying Amazon EC2 instances, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage the shared file system for session data storage.
Create an Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached) cluster, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage the cluster for session data storage.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB table, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage the table for session data storage.
questions.explanation: An Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached) cluster provides the lowest possible latency for session data because it is a purpose-built, distributed, in-memory store designed for exactly this kind of fast, externalized session access at scale. An RDS instance (A) or a shared file system across EC2 instances (B) both introduce higher latency than an in-memory cache due to disk-backed storage and additional access layers, and while DynamoDB (D) is also a valid, durable option for session storage, it does not achieve the lowest possible latency the way an in-memory cache purpose-built for this use case does.

questions.question: A developer has deployed an AWS Lambda function that is subscribed to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. The developer must implement a solution to add a record of each Lambda function invocation to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Which solution will meet this requirement?
options: Configure the SQS queue as a dead-letter queue for the Lambda function.
Create code that uses the AWS SDK to call the SQS SendMessage operation to add the invocation details to the SQS queue. Add the code to the end of the Lambda function.

Add two asynchronous invocation destinations to the Lambda function: one destination for successful invocations and one destination for failed invocations. Configure the SQS queue as the destination for each type. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm based on the DestinationDeliveryFailures metric to catch any message that cannot be delivered.

Add a single asynchronous invocation destination to the Lambda function to capture successful invocations. Configure the SQS queue as the destination. Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm based on the DestinationDeliveryFailures metric to catch any message that cannot be delivered.
questions.explanation: Configuring two asynchronous invocation destinations on the Lambda function, one for successful invocations and one for failed invocations, both pointed at the SQS queue, ensures a record of every invocation (success or failure) is added to the queue, and adding a CloudWatch alarm on the DestinationDeliveryFailures metric catches cases where even that destination delivery itself fails. Configuring the SQS queue only as a dead-letter queue (A) would record only failed invocations, not every invocation as required, manually calling SendMessage at the end of the function's own code (B) does not capture invocations where the function crashes before reaching that code, and configuring only the success destination (D) would miss recording failed invocations, which the requirement calls for as well.

questions.question: An AWS Lambda function that handles application requests uses the default Lambda logging mechanism to log the timestamp, processing time, and status of requests. A developer needs to create Amazon CloudWatch metrics based on the logs. The developer needs to write the metrics to a custom CloudWatch metrics namespace. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to generate custom metrics from the logs by using CloudWatch embedded metric format (EMF).
Use Amazon CloudWatch RUM to generate custom metrics from the logs by using CloudWatch embedded metric format (EMF).
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to generate custom metrics from the logs by using JSON format.
Use the CloudWatch embedded metric format (EMF) for the structure of the log statements to generate custom CloudWatch metrics.
questions.explanation: Writing log statements in CloudWatch embedded metric format lets CloudWatch extract metric values into a custom namespace directly from the log stream. Logs Insights queries analyze stored logs but do not publish new namespaced metrics by themselves; RUM monitors browser user experience rather than Lambda logs.

questions.question: A developer needs to configure an AWS Lambda function to make HTTP POST requests to an internal application. The application is in the same AWS account that hosts the function. The internal application runs on Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet within a VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure a VPC endpoint to connect to the private subnet. Attach the endpoint to the Lambda function.
Attach the Lambda function to the VPC and to the private subnet.
Configure a VPN connection between the Lambda function and the private subnet. Attach the VPN to the Lambda function.
Configure the VPC route table to include the Lambda function’s IP address.
questions.explanation: Attaching the Lambda function to the VPC and to the private subnet where the internal application's EC2 instances run lets the function reach the private application directly over the internal network, using standard Lambda VPC networking with no additional connectivity mechanism needed. There is no 'VPC endpoint to connect to a private subnet' concept the way described (A), a VPN connection between a Lambda function and a subnet (C) is not how Lambda establishes VPC connectivity, and manually editing a VPC route table to include a Lambda function's IP address (D) does not reflect how Lambda's elastic network interfaces work, since Lambda's VPC integration is configured directly on the function rather than through manual route table entries.

questions.question: A company has an application that processes audio files for different departments. When audio files are saved to an Amazon S3 bucket, an AWS Lambda function receives an event notification and processes the audio input. A developer needs to update the solution so that the application can process the audio files for each department independently. The application must publish the audio file location for each department to each department's existing Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Which solution will meet these requirements with no changes to the Lambda function code?
options: Configure the S3 bucket to send the event notifications to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe each department’s SQS queue to the SNS topic. Configure subscription filter policies.
Update the Lambda function to write the file location to a single shared SQS queue. Configure the shared SQS queue to send the file reference to each department’s SQS queue.
Update the Lambda function to send the file location to each department’s SQS queue.
Configure the S3 bucket to send the event notifications to each department’s SQS queue.
questions.explanation: Configuring the S3 bucket's event notifications to publish to a single Amazon SNS topic, then subscribing each department's existing SQS queue to that topic with a subscription filter policy scoped to that department, lets S3's existing notification mechanism fan out to all department queues without touching the Lambda function's code at all. Updating the Lambda function directly to write to each department's queue (C) or routing through a single shared queue that then forwards to each department queue (B) both require code changes the requirement explicitly rules out, and configuring the S3 bucket to send notifications to each department's SQS queue directly (D) does not support the described per-department filtering logic the way an SNS topic with subscription filter policies does.

questions.question: Two containerized microservices are hosted on Amazon EC2 ECS. The first microservice reads an Amazon RDS Aurora database instance, and the second microservice reads an Amazon DynamoDB table. How can each microservice be granted the minimum privileges?
options: Set ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM_ROLE to false on EC2 instance boot in ECS agent configuration file. Run the first microservice with an IAM role for ECS tasks with read-only access for the Aurora database. Run the second microservice with an IAM role for ECS tasks with read-only access to DynamoDB.
Set ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM ROLE to false on EC2 instance boot in the ECS agent configuration file. Grant the instance profile role read-only access to the Aurora database and DynamoDB.

Set ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM ROLE to true on EC2 instance boot in the ECS agent configuration file. Run the first microservice with an IAM role for ECS tasks with read-only access for the Aurora database. Run the second microservice with an IAM role for ECS tasks with read-only access to DynamoDB.
Set ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM_ROLE to true on EC2 instance boot in the ECS agent configuration file. Grant the instance profile role read-only access to the Aurora database and DynamoDB.
questions.explanation: Setting ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM_ROLE to true and running each microservice with its own dedicated IAM role for ECS tasks, scoped to only the specific data store it needs (read-only Aurora access for one, read-only DynamoDB access for the other), grants each task exactly the minimum privileges it requires. Setting ECS_ENABLE_TASK_IAM_ROLE to false (A, B) disables per-task IAM roles entirely, forcing both microservices to share whatever broader permissions are granted to the EC2 instance profile role instead, which violates least privilege by granting both services access to both data stores.

questions.question: A developer is writing a mobile application that allows users to view images from an S3 bucket. The users must be able to log in with their Amazon login, as well as supported social media accounts. How can the developer provide this authentication functionality?
options: Use Amazon Cognito with web identity federation.
Use Amazon Cognito with SAML-based identity federation.
Use IAM access keys and secret keys in the application code to allow Get* on the S3 bucket.
Use AWS STS AssumeRole in the application code and assume a role with Get* permissions on the S3 bucket.
questions.explanation: Amazon Cognito with web identity federation is designed to let users sign in with public identity providers, including Login with Amazon and other social providers, and then exchange that identity for scoped, temporary AWS credentials to access resources like S3. SAML-based federation (B) targets enterprise identity providers using the SAML 2.0 protocol rather than typical consumer social logins, and embedding long-lived IAM user access keys (C) or manually calling AssumeRole with an app-embedded role (D) both require the app to manage AWS credentials directly.

questions.question: An application that is running on Amazon EC2 instances stores data in an Amazon S3 bucket. All the data must be encrypted in transit. How can a developer ensure that all traffic to the S3 bucket is encrypted?
options: Install certificates on the EC2 instances.
Create a private VPC endpoint.
Configure the S3 bucket with server-side encryption with AWS KMS managed encryption keys (SSE-KMS).
Create an S3 bucket policy that denies traffic when the value for the aws:SecureTransport condition key is false.
questions.explanation: A bucket policy denying access when aws:SecureTransport is false is the standard S3 mechanism to enforce TLS-only access for every request, blocking any plaintext HTTP request regardless of the caller's other permissions. Installing certificates on EC2 instances (A) does not affect how the application talks to S3's own endpoint, a private VPC endpoint (B) keeps traffic off the public internet but does not by itself mandate HTTPS, and SSE-KMS (C) encrypts data at rest rather than the transport of the request.

questions.question: A company is hosting an Amazon AP! Gateway REST API that calls a single AWS Lambda function. The function is infrequently invoked by multiple clients at the same time. The code performance is optimal, but the company wants to optimize the startup time of the function What can a developer do to optimize the initialization of the function?
options: Enable API Gateway caching for the REST API.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function.
Use Lambda proxy integration for the REST API.
Configure AWS Global Accelerator for the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Configuring provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function pre-initializes execution environments ahead of invocations, which is exactly the mechanism to optimize the startup (cold start) time for an infrequently invoked function whose code performance is already optimal. Enabling API Gateway caching (A) caches response payloads, it does not reduce Lambda's own initialization time, Lambda proxy integration (C) is an integration format choice unrelated to cold starts, and AWS Global Accelerator (D) improves network path routing to endpoints, it does not affect a Lambda function's own initialization time.

questions.question: A developer is building a three-tier application with an Application Load Balancer (ALB), Amazon EC2 instances, and Amazon RDS. There is an alias record in Amazon Route 53 that points to the ALB. When the developer tries to access the ALB from a laptop, the request times out. Which logs should the developer investigate to verify that the request is reaching the AWS network?
options: VPC Flow Logs
Amazon Route 53 logs
AWS Systems Manager Agent logs
Amazon CloudWatch agent logs
questions.explanation: VPC Flow Logs show whether the laptop traffic reaches the VPC and where it is accepted or rejected, confirming network delivery toward the ALB. Route 53 logs cover DNS resolution rather than TCP delivery; Systems Manager and CloudWatch agent logs describe host software rather than inbound packet flow.

questions.question: A developer has an application that uses AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS). The application calls the STS AssumeRole API operation to provide trusted users with temporary security credentials. The application calls AWS STS at the service's default endpoint: https://sts.amazonaws.com. The application is deployed in an Asia Pacific AWS Region. The application is experiencing errors that are related to intermittent latency when the application calls AWS STS. What should the developer do to resolve this issue?
options: Update the application to use the GetSessionToken API operation.
Update the application to use the AssumeRoleWithSAML API operation.
Update the application to use a Regional STS endpoint that is closer to the application deployment.
Update the application to use the AssumeRoleWithWebldentity API operation. Move the STS endpoint to a global endpoint.
questions.explanation: Regional STS endpoints reduce latency by serving AssumeRole calls from an AWS Region physically closer to the calling application instead of always routing through the legacy global endpoint hosted in us-east-1, directly addressing latency experienced from an Asia Pacific deployment. GetSessionToken (A) is a different operation for a different use case, AssumeRoleWithSAML (B) is for SAML federation flows unrelated to the latency issue, and there is no action to 'move the STS endpoint to a global endpoint' for AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (D); that is the opposite of the fix, since the global endpoint is the source of the latency.

questions.question: A company is launching a photo sharing application on AWS. Users use the application to upload images to an Amazon S3 bucket. When users upload images, an AWS Lambda function creates thumbnail versions of the images and stores the thumbnail versions in another S3 bucket. During development, a developer notices that the Lambda function takes more than 2 minutes to complete the thumbnail process. The company needs alll images to be processed in less than 30 seconds. What should the developer do to meet these requirements?
options: Increase the virtual CPUs (vCPUs) for the Lambda function to use 10 vCPUs.
Change Lambda function instance type to use m6a.4xlarge.
Configure the Lambda function to increase the amount of memory.
Configure burstable performance for the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: Increasing the amount of memory allocated to the Lambda function proportionally increases its available CPU power, since Lambda scales vCPU allocation with configured memory, which directly speeds up a compute-bound image-processing task like thumbnail generation. There is no separate 'vCPU count' setting to configure directly (A), Lambda functions do not run on selectable EC2 instance types like m6a.4xlarge (B), and Lambda does not have a distinct 'burstable performance' configuration option the way certain EC2 instance types do (D).

questions.question: A development team is designing a mobile app that requires multi-factor authentication. Which steps should be taken to achieve this? (Choose two.)
options: Use Amazon Cognito to create a user pool and create users in the user pool.
Send multi-factor authentication text codes to users with the Amazon SNS Publish API call in the app code.
Enable multi-factor authentication for the Amazon Cognito user pool.
Use AWS IAM to create IAM users.
Enable multifactor authentication for the users created in AWS IAM.
questions.explanation: Amazon Cognito user pools have built-in support for enforcing multi-factor authentication as a pool setting, handling the challenge flow natively without custom code. Manually sending MFA codes through direct SNS Publish calls in application code (B) reimplements what Cognito's built-in MFA already does, and while IAM does support MFA for IAM users (D, E), IAM users are meant for AWS account access rather than a mobile app's own end-user base, which is what Cognito user pools are designed for.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that will process messages from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) standard queue. The application needs to process the messages in an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task. Which actions will result in the MOST cost-effective processing of the messages? (Choose two.)
options: Use long polling to query the queue for new messages.
Use short polling to query the queue for new messages.
Use message batching to retrieve messages from the queue.
Use Amazon ElastiCache to cache messages in the queue.
Use an SQS FIFO queue to manage the messages.
questions.explanation: Long polling reduces the number of empty responses (and thus the number of billed SQS API requests) by waiting for messages to arrive rather than returning immediately, and message batching retrieves and processes multiple messages per request, both directly reducing the total number of SQS API calls needed and therefore the cost of processing the queue. Short polling (B) increases the number of empty, billed requests compared to long polling, ElastiCache (D) is an unrelated in-memory cache with no built-in role in consuming an SQS queue, and switching to a FIFO queue (E) addresses ordering and deduplication, not the cost-efficiency of polling itself.

questions.question: A developer is writing an application in AWS Lambda. To simplify testing and deployments, the developer needs the database connection string to be easily changed without modifying the Lambda code. How can this requirement be met?
options: Store the connection string as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager.
Store the connection string in an IAM user account.
Store the connection string in AWS KMS.
Store the connection string as a Lambda layer.
questions.explanation: Storing the connection string in Secrets Manager lets it be updated independently of the Lambda function's code or deployment package, with the function simply retrieving the current value at runtime through the SDK. Storing it in an IAM user account (B) is not a valid place to store configuration data, AWS KMS (C) is a key-management service for encryption operations rather than a store for arbitrary strings, and a Lambda layer (D) bundles shared code into the deployment package, so updating a value there still requires publishing a new layer version and updating the function.

questions.question: A developer is building an ecommerce application that uses multiple AWS Lambda functions. Each function performs a specific step in a customer order workflow, such as order processing and inventory management. The developer must ensure that the Lambda functions run in a specific order. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Configure an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue to contain messages about each step a function must perform. Configure the Lambda functions to run sequentially based on the order of messages in the SQS queue.

Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to contain notifications about each step a function must perform. Subscribe the Lambda functions to the SNS topic. Use subscription filters based on the step each function must perform.
Configure an AWS Step Functions state machine to invoke the Lambda functions in a specific order.
Configure Amazon EventBridge Scheduler schedules to invoke the Lambda functions in a specific order.
questions.explanation: An AWS Step Functions state machine is purpose-built to orchestrate multiple Lambda functions in a defined, managed sequence, directly enforcing the required order with the least operational overhead since no custom message-based coordination needs to be built or maintained. Using an SQS queue's message order to imply execution order (A) does not guarantee the Lambda functions themselves run only in that order without additional custom logic, an SNS topic with subscription filters (B) is designed for fan-out message routing rather than enforcing sequential execution, and scheduling independent EventBridge Scheduler invocations (D) does not coordinate a strict dependency chain between the functions the way a state machine's explicit sequence does.

questions.question: A developer is building an image-processing application that includes an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function moves images from one AWS service to another AWS service for image processing. For images that are larger than 2 MB, the Lambda function returns the following error: “Task timed out after 3.01 seconds.” The developer needs to resolve the error without modifying the Lambda function code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Increase the Lambda function’s timeout value.
Configure the Lambda function to not move images that are larger than 2 MB.
Request a concurrency quota increase for the Lambda function.
Configure provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function.
questions.explanation: The 3.01-second timeout shows the function simply runs out of time on larger images, so raising the timeout without touching code lets the existing move logic finish. Skipping large images drops required work; concurrency quotas control parallelism rather than single-invocation duration; provisioned concurrency warms environments but does not extend the time limit.

questions.question: A developer has an application container, an AWS Lambda function, and an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The Lambda function uses the SQS queue as an event source. The Lambda function makes a call to a third-party machine learning API when the function is invoked. The response from the third-party API can take up to 60 seconds to return. The Lambda function's timeout value is currently 65 seconds. The developer has noticed that the Lambda function sometimes processes duplicate messages from the SQS queue. What should the developer do to ensure that the Lambda function does not process duplicate messages?
options: Configure the Lambda function with a larger amount of memory.
Configure an increase in the Lambda function’s timeout value.
Configure the SQS queue’s delivery delay value to be greater than the maximum time it takes to call the third-party API.
Configure the SQS queue’s visibility timeout value to be greater than the maximum time it takes to call the third-party API.
questions.explanation: Configuring the SQS queue's visibility timeout to exceed the maximum time the third-party API call can take (up to 60 seconds) ensures a message stays hidden from other consumers for the entire time it takes to process, so it cannot become visible again and be picked up a second time while the first invocation is still waiting on the slow API call. Increasing memory (A) or the Lambda timeout (B) do not address the actual cause, which is the message becoming visible again before processing finishes, and increasing the queue's delivery delay (C) only affects how long a message waits before its very first delivery, it does not prevent redelivery during an in-progress, still-running invocation.

questions.question: A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances. The application needs to use dynamic feature flags that will be shared with other applications. The application must poll on an interval for new feature flag values. The values must be cached when they are retrieved. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
options: Store the feature flag values in AWS Secrets Manager. Configure an Amazon ElastiCache node to cache the values by using a lazy loading strategy in the application. Update the application to poll for the values on an interval from ElastiCache.

Store the feature flag values in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Configure DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to cache the values by using a lazy loading strategy in the application. Update the application to poll for the values on an interval from DynamoDB.

Store the feature flag values in AWS AppConfig. Configure AWS AppConfig Agent on the EC2 instances to poll for the values on an interval. Update the application to retrieve the values from the AppConfig Agent localhost endpoint.

Store the feature flag values in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Configure the application to poll on an interval. Configure the application to use the AWS SDK to retrieve the values from Parameter Store and to store the values in memory.
questions.explanation: AWS AppConfig, with its Agent running locally on the EC2 instances polling for updated values and caching them, is a fully managed, purpose-built feature-flag service that natively supports polling on an interval and local caching without the application needing to build its own polling or caching logic, retrieving values from the Agent's localhost endpoint. Secrets Manager (A) and Parameter Store (D) are not purpose-built feature-flag services and would each require the application itself to implement polling and caching logic, and DynamoDB with DAX (B) misapplies a database-acceleration cache to what is fundamentally a configuration/feature-flag use case that AppConfig already directly serves.

questions.question: A team deploys an AWS CloudFormation template to update a stack that already included an Amazon DynamoDB table. However, before the deployment of the update, the team changed the name of the DynamoDB table on the template by mistake. The DeletionPolicy attribute for all resources has the default value. What will be the result of this mistake?
options: CloudFormation will create a new table and will delete the existing table.
CloudFormation will create a new table and will keep the existing table.
CloudFormation will overwrite the existing table and will rename the existing table.
CloudFormation will keep the existing table and will not create a new table.
questions.explanation: Since the developer changed the DynamoDB table's logical name/properties in the template (a change CloudFormation treats as requiring replacement) and the DeletionPolicy is left at its default value (Delete), CloudFormation will provision a brand-new table under the new name/configuration and then delete the original table that is no longer referenced by the template. If a DeletionPolicy of Retain had been set (B, D), CloudFormation would have kept the original table alongside the new one instead of deleting it, and CloudFormation does not simply 'overwrite and rename' an existing table in place for this kind of replacement-triggering change (C), nor does it leave the old table untouched with no new table created (D), since the template change requires provisioning a genuinely new resource.

questions.question: A developer is deploying an application on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster that uses AWS Fargate. The developer is using a Docker container with an Ubuntu image. The developer needs to implement a solution to store application data that is available from multiple ECS tasks. The application data must remain accessible after the container is terminated. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Attach an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server volume to the container definition.
Specify the DockerVolumeConfiguration parameter in the ECS task definition to attach a Docker volume.
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. Specify the mountPoints attribute and the efsVolumeConfiguration attribute in the ECS task definition.
Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Specify the mount point configuration in the ECS task definition.
questions.explanation: Creating an Amazon EFS file system and specifying the mountPoints and efsVolumeConfiguration attributes in the ECS task definition lets Fargate tasks mount a shared, durable, network file system whose data persists independently of any single task's lifecycle and remains accessible to multiple concurrently running ECS tasks. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server (A) is designed for Windows-based SMB workloads, not a natural fit for an Ubuntu-based container, a Docker volume via DockerVolumeConfiguration (B) is tied to the underlying host and is not supported the way described on Fargate (which abstracts away the host), and an EBS volume (D) attaches to a single compute resource at a time and does not natively support simultaneous shared access from multiple ECS tasks the way EFS does.

questions.question: A developer is creating an AWS Lambda function that needs network access to private resources in a VPC. Which solution will provide this access with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Attach the Lambda function to the VPC through private subnets. Create a security group that allows network access to the private resources. Associate the security group with the Lambda function.

Configure the Lambda function to route traffic through a VPN connection. Create a security group that allows network access to the private resources. Associate the security group with the Lambda function.
Configure a VPC endpoint connection for the Lambda function. Set up the VPC endpoint to route traffic through a NAT gateway.
Configure an AWS PrivateLink endpoint for the private resources. Configure the Lambda function to reference the PrivateLink endpoint.
questions.explanation: Attaching the Lambda function to the VPC through private subnets, with a security group permitting the needed network access, is the standard, lowest-overhead way to give a Lambda function connectivity to private VPC resources, since Lambda natively supports VPC attachment with no additional networking components required. Lambda functions do not route traffic through a VPN connection as a configuration option (B), a VPC endpoint routed through a NAT gateway (C) conflates two unrelated networking concepts and is not how Lambda VPC access works, and AWS PrivateLink (D) is used to privately expose specific services to consumers, it is not the mechanism used to grant a Lambda function outbound access to arbitrary private VPC resources.

questions.question: A developer needs to automate deployments for a serverless, event-based workload. The developer needs to create standardized templates to define the infrastructure and to test the functionality of the workload locally before deployment The developer already uses a pipeline in AWS CodePipeline. The developer needs to incorporate any other infrastructure changes into the existing pipeline. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Create an AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) template. Configure the pipeline stages in CodePipeline to run the necessary AWS SAM CLI commands to deploy the serverless workload.
Create an AWS Step Functions workflow template based on the infrastructure by using the Amazon States Language. Start the Step Functions state machine from the existing pipeline.
Create an AWS CloudFormation template. Use the existing pipeline workflow to build a pipeline for AWS CloudFormation stacks.
Create an AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) template. Use an automated script to deploy the serverless workload by using the AWS SAM CLI deploy command.
questions.explanation: Creating an AWS SAM template (which supports local testing via the SAM CLI and standardized infrastructure-as-code for a serverless, event-driven workload) and configuring the existing CodePipeline stages to run the necessary SAM CLI commands integrates infrastructure deployment directly into the existing pipeline with no new orchestration tool needed. A Step Functions workflow describing infrastructure via the Amazon States Language (B) is not how infrastructure is defined or deployed, that's what CloudFormation/SAM templates are for, a raw CloudFormation template without SAM's added local-testing and serverless-specific tooling (C) does not support local functionality testing as directly as SAM does, and using an automated script to call sam deploy outside of (rather than incorporated into) the existing CodePipeline pipeline (D) does not integrate the change into the existing pipeline as required.

questions.question: A developer is creating a stock trading application. The developer needs a solution to send text messages to application users to confirmation when a trade has been completed. The solution must deliver messages in the order a user makes stock trades. The solution must not send duplicate messages. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure the application to publish messages to an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream. Configure the delivery stream to have a destination of each user’s mobile phone number that is passed in the trade confirmation message.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue. Use the SendMessageIn API call to send the trade confirmation messages to the queue. Use the SendMessageOut API to send the messages to users by using the information provided in the trade confirmation message.

Configure a pipe in Amazon EventBridge Pipes. Connect the application to the pipe as a source. Configure the pipe to use each user’s mobile phone number as a target. Configure the pipe to send incoming events to the users.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) FIFO topic. Configure the application to use the AWS SDK to publish notifications to the SNS topic to send SMS messages to the users.
questions.explanation: An SNS FIFO topic preserves strict message ordering per message group and provides built-in deduplication, and the AWS SDK can publish directly to it to send SMS notifications to users, meeting both the in-order delivery and no-duplicate-messages requirements natively. Amazon Data Firehose (A) is designed for streaming delivery to storage and analytics destinations, not for sending SMS notifications to individual phone numbers, a standard SQS queue with custom 'SendMessageIn/SendMessageOut' API calls (B, these are not real SQS API operations) does not describe an actual SQS mechanism, and an EventBridge pipe targeting mobile phone numbers directly (C) is not a supported EventBridge Pipes target type for sending SMS messages.

questions.question: A developer is deploying a new Node.js AWS Lambda function that is not connected to a VPC. The Lambda function needs to connect to and query an Amazon Aurora database that is not publicly accessible. The developer is expecting unpredictable surges in database traffic. What should the developer do to give the Lambda function access to the database?
options: Configure the Lambda function to use an Amazon RDS proxy.
Configure a NAT gateway. Attach the NAT gateway to the Lambda function.
Enable public access on the Aurora database. Configure a security group on the database to allow outbound access for the database engine’s port.
Enable VPC access for the Lambda function. Attach the Lambda function to a new security group that does not have rules.
questions.explanation: Configuring the Lambda function to use an Amazon RDS Proxy lets it connect to and query the private Aurora database through a managed, pooled, and automatically scaling connection layer, without needing the Lambda function itself to be attached to a VPC, which is well suited to unpredictable traffic surges since RDS Proxy handles connection scaling on the function's behalf. Attaching a NAT gateway directly to a Lambda function (B) is not how Lambda networking works, making the Aurora database publicly accessible (C) directly contradicts the requirement that it not be publicly accessible, and attaching Lambda to a VPC with an empty security group that has no rules (D) would not actually grant any network access to the database at all, since a security group with no rules permits nothing.

questions.question: A company generates SSL certificates from a third-party provider. The company imports the certificates into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) to use with public web applications. A developer must implement a solution to notify the company’s security team 90 days before an imported certificate expires. The company already has configured an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The company also has configured an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that has the security team’s email address as a subscriber. Which solution will provide the security team with the required notification about certificates?
options: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that specifies the ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event type. Set the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule’s target.

Create an AWS Lambda function to search for all certificates that are expiring within 90 days. Program the Lambda function to send each identified certificate’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in a message to the SQS queue.

Create an AWS Step Functions workflow that is invoked by each certificate’s expiration notification from AWS CloudTrail. Create an AWS Lambda function to send each certificate's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in a message to the SQS queue.

Configure AWS Config with the acm-certificate-expiration-check managed rule to run every 24 hours. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that includes an event pattern that specifies the Config Rules Compliance Change detail type and the configured rule. Set the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule’s target.
questions.explanation: An EventBridge rule that matches the ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event type, with the existing SNS topic (which already has the security team subscribed by email) as its target, uses ACM's own native expiration event and requires no custom code to detect expiring certificates or determine the 90-day threshold, since ACM's managed monitoring already emits this event automatically. Building a custom Lambda function to search for expiring certificates (B) reimplements detection logic ACM already provides as a native event, and routing through a Step Functions workflow invoked from CloudTrail (C) is a heavier, more custom mechanism than simply targeting the existing SNS topic directly from the native ACM EventBridge event.

questions.question: A company uses two AWS accounts: production and development. The company stores data in an Amazon S3 bucket that is in the production account. The data is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key. The company plans to copy the data to another S3 bucket that is in the development account. A developer needs to use a KMS key to encrypt the data in the S3 bucket that is in the development account. The KMS key in the development account must be accessible from the production account, Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Replicate the customer managed KMS key from the production account to the development account. Specify the production account in the key policy.
Create a new customer managed KMS key in the development account. Specify the production account in the key policy.
Create a new AWS managed KMS key for Amazon S3 in the development account. Specify the production account in the key policy.
Replicate the default AWS managed KMS key for Amazon S3 from the production account to the development account. Specify the production account in the key policy.
questions.explanation: KMS keys are Regional, account-scoped resources that cannot be copied across accounts, so the only way to encrypt data in the development account's S3 bucket with a KMS key usable there is to create a new customer managed key in that account, whose key policy then grants the production account's principals permission to use it. There is no operation to replicate a customer managed KMS key across accounts (A, D), and an AWS managed key for S3 (C) does not have a customer-editable key policy that could grant another account access.

questions.question: A developer is using AWS CodeDeploy to launch an application onto Amazon EC2 instances. The application deployment fails during testing. The developer notices an IAM_ROLE_PERMISSIONS error code in Amazon CloudWatch logs. What should the developer do to resolve the error?
options: Ensure that the deployment group is using the correct role name for the CodeDeploy service role.
Attach the AWSCodeDeployRoleECS policy to the CodeDeploy service role.
Attach the AWSCodeDeployRole policy to the CodeDeploy service role.
Ensure the CodeDeploy agent is installed and running on all instances in the deployment group.
questions.explanation: An IAM_ROLE_PERMISSIONS error from CodeDeploy specifically indicates the CodeDeploy service role itself is missing required permissions, and attaching the AWS-managed AWSCodeDeployRole policy (the standard managed policy granting CodeDeploy the EC2 and Auto Scaling permissions it needs to perform deployments) to that service role is the documented fix. AWSCodeDeployRoleECS (B) is the managed policy for ECS-based (not EC2-based) CodeDeploy deployments, which does not match this EC2 instance deployment scenario, checking the deployment group's role name (A) addresses a different kind of misconfiguration than a genuine permissions gap, and ensuring the CodeDeploy agent is installed and running (D) would produce a different error related to agent connectivity, not an IAM_ROLE_PERMISSIONS error.

questions.question: A company wants to send notifications to customers to advertise a sale on the company’s products. The company needs to use Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) FIFO topics. The company needs to examine the rate at which the topics send notifications and the latency with which the topics send notifications. Which solution will meet these requirements with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Use AWS X-Ray. Enable active tracing for Amazon SNS.
Use the Amazon CloudWatch NumberOfNotificationsFailed metric.
Use AWS CloudTrail to log all Amazon SNS API calls.
Use Amazon GuardDuty. Enable runtime monitoring.
questions.explanation: Enabling active tracing for SNS feeds publish and delivery spans into X-Ray, which exposes per-topic throughput rates and end-to-end notification latency with minimal extra plumbing. Failed-notification counts alone omit latency; CloudTrail logs API calls rather than delivery timing; GuardDuty is threat detection rather than messaging observability.

questions.question: A cloud-based video surveillance company is developing an application that analyzes video files. After the application analyzes the files, the company can discard the files. The company stores the files in an Amazon S3 bucket. The files are 1 GB in size on average. No file is larger than 2 GB. An AWS Lambda function will run one time for each video file that is processed. The processing is very I/O intensive, and the application must read each file multiple times. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST performance-optimized way?
options: Attach an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume that is larger than 1 GB to the Lambda function. Copy the files from the S3 bucket to the EBS volume.
Attach an Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) to the Lambda function. Use the ENA to read the video files from the S3 bucket.
Increase the ephemeral storage size to 2 GB. Copy the files from the S3 bucket to the /tmp directory of the Lambda function.
Configure the Lambda function code to read the video files directly from the S3 bucket.
questions.explanation: Increasing the Lambda function's ephemeral storage to 2 GB and copying each video file (up to 2 GB) into the local /tmp directory lets the I/O-intensive processing repeatedly read the file from fast local storage rather than repeatedly reading it over the network from S3, which is the most performance-optimized option given the requirement to read each file multiple times. Attaching an EBS volume to a Lambda function (A) is not a supported Lambda storage attachment mechanism, attaching an Elastic Network Adapter (B) is an EC2 networking concept unrelated to how Lambda reads from S3, and reading the video files directly from S3 on every access (D) means repeatedly incurring network latency for an I/O-intensive workload that needs to read the same file multiple times.

questions.question: A company stores customer credit reports in an Amazon S3 bucket. An analytics service uses standard Amazon S3 GET requests to access the reports. A developer must implement a solution to redact personally identifiable information (PII) from the reports before the reports reach the analytics service. Which solution will meet this requirement with the MOST operational efficiency?
options: Load the S3 objects into Amazon Redshift by using a COPY command. Implement dynamic data masking. Refactor the analytics service to read from Amazon Redshift.
Set up an S3 Object Lambda function. Attach the function to an S3 Object Lambda Access Point. Program the function to call a PII redaction API.
Use AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) to implement encryption in the S3 bucket. Re-upload all the existing S3 objects. Give the kms:Decrypt permission to the analytics service.
Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Implement message data protection. Refactor the analytics service to publish data access requests to the SNS topic.
questions.explanation: As with S3 Object Lambda used elsewhere in this exam, this is the standard pattern for transforming a GetObject response, redacting PII here, on the fly for a specific consumer without duplicating or re-uploading the underlying object, and it requires no change to how the analytics service issues standard S3 GET requests. Loading data into Redshift with dynamic data masking (A) requires standing up a separate analytics pipeline, encrypting the bucket with KMS and granting kms:Decrypt (C) gives the analytics service the full unredacted data, and routing through an SNS topic with message data protection (D) is designed for pub/sub payloads rather than transforming S3 GET responses.

questions.question: A company is using the AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) to develop a social media application. A developer needs a quick way to test AWS Lambda functions locally by using test event payloads. The developer needs the structure of these test event payloads to match the actual events that AWS services create. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
options: Create shareable test Lambda events. Use these test Lambda events for local testing.
Store manually created test event payloads locally. Use the sam local invoke command with the file path to the payloads.
Store manually created test event payloads in an Amazon S3 bucket. Use the sam local invoke command with the S3 path to the payloads.
Use the sam local generate-event command to create test payloads for local testing.
questions.explanation: The sam local generate-event command produces sample event payloads that are structurally accurate to the real events actual AWS services generate (such as S3, API Gateway, or SNS events), letting the developer immediately test Lambda functions locally against realistic data with a single built-in SAM CLI command and no manual event-crafting effort. Shareable test Lambda events (A) are console-managed test events for testing in the AWS Lambda console rather than for local testing, and manually creating event payloads and storing them locally or in S3 (B, C) both require the developer to hand-author the event structure themselves rather than using SAM's built-in generator for accurate, realistic events.

questions.question: A developer is building the authentication mechanism for a new mobile app. Users need to be able to sign up, sign in, and access secured backend AWS resources. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Use AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer to generate IAM policies. Create an IAM role. Attach the policies to the role. Integrate the IAM role with an identity provider that the mobile app uses.

Create an IAM policy that grants access to the backend resources. Create an IAM role. Attach the policy to the role. Create an Amazon API Gateway endpoint. Attach the role to the endpoint. Integrate the endpoint with the mobile app.

Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool. Configure permissions by choosing a default IAM role for authenticated users or guest users in the identity pool. Associate the identity pool with an identity provider. Integrate the identity pool with the mobile app.

Create an Amazon Cognito user pool. Configure the security requirements by choosing a password policy, multi-factor authentication (MFA) requirements, and user account recovery options. Create an app client. Integrate the app client with the mobile app.
questions.explanation: A Cognito user pool is the full user-directory and authentication service supporting sign-up, sign-in, configurable password policies, MFA, and account recovery, and an app client is how a mobile app integrates with it. IAM Access Analyzer (A) is a policy-generation and validation tool rather than an end-user authentication service, manually building an IAM role and API Gateway combination (B) provides no user directory for individual sign-up, and a Cognito identity pool alone (C) only exchanges an existing identity for AWS credentials, it does not handle user registration or password policies.

questions.question: A developer is designing an event-driven architecture. An AWS Lambda function that processes data needs to push processed data to a subset of four consumer Lambda functions. The data must be routed based on the value of one field in the data. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue and event source mapping for each consumer Lambda function. Add message routing logic to the data-processing Lambda function.

Create an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe the four consumer Lambda functions to the topic. Add message filtering logic to each consumer Lambda function. Subscribe the data-processing Lambda function to the SNS topic.

Create a separate Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic and subscription for each consumer Lambda function. Add message routing logic to the data-processing Lambda function to publish to the appropriate topic.

Create a single Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic. Subscribe the four consumer Lambda functions to the topic. Add SNS subscription filter policies to each subscription. Configure the data-processing Lambda function to publish to the topic.
questions.explanation: Publishing to a single SNS topic, with each of the four consumer Lambda functions subscribed using its own SNS subscription filter policy keyed on the routing field's value, lets SNS itself deliver each message only to the matching consumer(s) with no custom routing logic to write or maintain, the least operational overhead. Using a separate SQS queue and event source mapping per consumer with routing logic built into the data-processing function (A) requires writing and maintaining custom routing code, and separate SNS topics or subscriptions per consumer with routing logic in the publisher (C) or unfiltered subscriptions with per-consumer filtering logic (B) both push routing responsibility into custom code that a single topic with subscription filter policies already handles declaratively.

questions.question: A developer is creating a new application that will give users the ability to upload documents to Amazon S3. The contents of the documents must not be accessible to any third party. Which type of encryption will meet this requirement?
options: Client-side encryption by using the S3 Encryption Client with a Raw RSA wrapping key that is stored on the user’s device
Server-side encryption with S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
Dual-layer server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (DSSE-KMS)
questions.explanation: SSE-KMS gives the developer control over the KMS key's key policy, so access to decrypt and therefore read the document contents can be tightly restricted so that no unintended third party can access the plaintext. SSE-S3 (B) uses an S3-managed key with no customer control over the key policy, and while client-side encryption with a user-held key (A) and dual-layer KMS encryption (D) are also strong options, SSE-KMS is the more direct fit for restricting access purely through a customer-controlled key policy.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that consists of many AWS Lambda functions. The Lambda functions connect to a single Amazon RDS database. The developer needs to implement a solution to store the database credentials securely. When the credentials are updated, the Lambda functions must be able to use the new credentials without requiring a code update or a configuration update. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Store the credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Access the secret at runtime from within the Lambda functions.
Store the credentials as a secret in AWS Secrets Manager. Access the credentials in environment variables by using the containerDefinitions and valueFrom elements in reference to the secret value.
Store the credentials as a SecureString parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Add a trigger to pass the credentials to the Lambda functions when the Lambda functions run.
Store the credentials as a SecureString parameter in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Add a reference to the parameter in an environment variable in the Lambda functions.
questions.explanation: Retrieving the secret directly from Secrets Manager inside the Lambda function's code at runtime means every invocation, across all functions, always reads the current credential value, so a rotation is picked up immediately with no code or configuration change anywhere. The containerDefinitions/valueFrom pattern (B) is an ECS task-definition mechanism for injecting secrets into containers, not applicable to Lambda, and both Parameter Store options (C, D) either misstate its capabilities or would still require an explicit environment-variable update to reflect newly rotated values.

questions.question: A developer is building an application that stores sensitive user data. The application includes an Amazon CloudFront distribution and multiple AWS Lambda functions that handle user requests. The user requests contain over 20 data fields. Each application transaction contains sensitive data that must be encrypted. Only specific parts of the application need to have the ability to decrypt the data. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Associate the CloudFront distribution with a Lambda@Edge function. Configure the function to perform field-level asymmetric encryption by using a user-defined RSA public key that is stored in AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).
Integrate AWS WAF with CloudFront to protect the sensitive data. Use a Lambda function and self-managed keys to perform the encryption and decryption processes.

Configure the CloudFront distribution to use WebSockets by forwarding all viewer request headers to the origin. Create an asymmetric AWS KMS key. Configure the CloudFront distribution to use field-level encryption. Use the AWS KMS key.

Configure the cache behavior in the CloudFront distribution to require HTTPS for communication between viewers and CloudFront. Configure GoudFront to require users to access the files by using either signed URLs or signed cookies.
questions.explanation: CloudFront's field-level encryption feature encrypts only specific sensitive request fields using a public key so that only backend components holding the corresponding private key can decrypt those particular fields, matching the requirement that only specific parts of the application can decrypt the data. A Lambda function with self-managed keys behind AWS WAF (B) reimplements what field-level encryption already provides, forwarding all headers over WebSockets (C) does not scope decryption ability to select parts of the application, and requiring HTTPS with signed URLs or cookies (D) secures transport and file access rather than selective per-field encryption of transaction data.

questions.question: An application includes an Amazon DynamoDB table that is named orders. The table has a primary partition key of id and a global secondary index (GSI) that is named an accountIndex. The GSI has a partition key of accountId and a sort key of orderDateTime. A developer needs to create an AWS Lambda function to retrieve the orders that have an accountId of 100. Which solution will meet this requirement by using the LEAST read capacity?
options: Define a DynamoDB API request for the GetItem action with the following parameters:
Define a DynamoDB API request for the BatchGetItem action with the following parameters:
Define a DynamoDB API request for the Scan action with the following parameters:
Define a DynamoDB API request for the Query action with the following parameters:
questions.explanation: The DynamoDB Query action, run against the accountIndex GSI with accountId as the partition key, retrieves exactly the matching orders for account 100 by reading only the relevant index partition, which consumes far less read capacity than reading through unrelated items.
